en: The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Sun’s Radiance Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Western Jin lay devotee Nie Chengyuan.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Vaiśālī at the Nāḍika Grove, together with a great [assembly].

Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus numbering eighteen thousand and eighty thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom were great sages who had attained supernormal powers, had fully acquired the dhāraṇīs and grasped the wisdom of the ten powers, dwelt in non-abiding while transcending the three gates of liberation, and whose skillful means and expedients were such that none failed to follow their transformation; whose wisdom of the threefold penetration was unimpeded, who traversed the three periods of time as peerless and solitary sovereigns, who perceived the origin and end of birth and death, who administered medicine according to the illness to ensure each found their proper place, who guarded the city of the Dharma and rescued all living beings, practicing the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and establishing bridges at appropriate times through the four debts of gratitude.

Through the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; by understanding the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they attain the patience of non-arising. They manifest entry among sentient beings without giving rise to any [discriminative] thoughts, instructing those who would regress so that they do not turn back. By means of the eight inconceivables, they deliver others from the eight difficulties. Unifying with the Dharma-body, they manifest as bodhisattvas, or as tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—just as sunlight shines everywhere, yet their coming and going throughout the ten directions involves no circling.

They contemplate all phenomena as being like transformations, illusions, dreams, mirages, echoes, and shadows—utterly non-existent. Gain and loss, defamation and praise, suffering and pleasure, good and evil are forever extinguished; they have transcended all worldly phenomena and reached the site of enlightenment, where all things are equal, without increase or decrease. Their names are as follows:

Bodhisattva Universal Radiance, Bodhisattva Universal Attainment, Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom, Bodhisattva Universal Intelligence, Bodhisattva Universal Arrival, Bodhisattva Radiance, Bodhisattva Blazing Light, Bodhisattva Equal Light, Bodhisattva Light-Essence, Bodhisattva Light-Creator, Bodhisattva Compassionate Light, Bodhisattva Compassionate Giving, Bodhisattva Compassionate Precepts, Bodhisattva Compassionate Patience, Bodhisattva Compassionate Diligence, Bodhisattva Compassionate Tranquility, Bodhisattva Compassionate Wisdom, Bodhisattva Compassionate Rescue, Bodhisattva Compassionate Protection, Bodhisattva Compassionate Rain, Bodhisattva Compassionate Clarity, and Bodhisattva Compassionate Universality.
All such foremost qualities, numbering eighty thousand, were likewise thus!

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of followers, and he preached the Dharma for them, expounding upon the infinite wisdom of the Mahāyāna practice.

At that time, there was a great elder in the city named Subhūti, who, together with a thousand followers, each holding a flower made of the seven precious gems, came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, scattering those precious flowers over the Buddha, each made this vow:
“May all classes of sentient beings in the ten directions have hearts as supple as these flowers and minds as pure as space.”
By the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, all those precious flowers were caused to float in mid-air and coalesce above the World-Honored One to form a flower canopy;
the light of this canopy shone universally upon the bodhisattvas in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, such that no devas or humans failed to behold it.
From each of the Buddha-worlds, countless hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and sat to one side.

Thereupon, eighty thousand great beings of universal compassion, along with ten billion Śakras and Brahmā kings, thirty billion Brahmā and various celestial deities and sublime gods, ten billion retinues of Śuddhāvāsa gods, twenty billion attendants, māra-sons, and guides, and five thousand billion playful celestial maidens, all followed one another to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

King Ajātaśatru with eighty thousand people, King Prasenajit with fifty thousand people, the King of Vaiśālī with eighty-four thousand venerable ones, King Udayana with twenty thousand people, King Śuddhodana with ninety thousand people, and King Kauśinagara with sixty thousand people—these kings, each leading their retinues in numbers beyond reckoning, all came together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—in incalculable billions beyond comparison—came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and each took their respective place, some sitting and some standing.

The Buddha stands among the assembly with a majestic power that is exceptionally venerable; he is like the sun first rising, or like the moon among the stars, and like Mount Sumeru towering above the great ocean, illuminating the four quarters.

The World-Honored One emits a majestic radiance from his body; his noble wisdom is boundless, universally illuminating all things so that none fail to receive deliverance. As the four classes of beings gaze upon him in reverence, it is as if those in darkness behold the light.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantaprabha. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha in verse:
"Greatly compassionate and pitying the masses, For those blinded by the veils of the aggregates;
Opening the eyes of the sightless to see, Transforming the unheard through the light of the Way."
Dwelling in the world like space, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water;
With a mind pure and transcending these, I prostrate and pay homage to the Unsurpassed Sage.

Contemplate that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, like a mirage, the moon reflected in water, a shadow, an echo, a magical illusion, or a plantain tree; understand that the three realms are likewise so!
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, you have accumulated merits beyond counting;
through the vast transformation of your compassionate mind and meditative equanimity, all classes of sentient beings are sustained by your grace.
Having realized that the three realms are like a dream, upon awakening they are all extinguished, with neither preference nor aversion;
birth and death are my own beginning and end—this is but a fleeting illusion, nothing at all.
The Buddha’s radiance shines everywhere, and his majestic marks and signs are beyond measure;
the Way is sublime and peerless—therefore, I bow my head in homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Originally I resolved my mind for the sake of the ten directions, to rescue those in distress and save the multitudes;
now that my vow has been fulfilled beyond measure, there is no one among all people who does not receive its benefit.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power; He attained immeasurable awakening and fulfilled the Way.
Understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally natural, He sought nothing from heterodox arts.
The multitude offered seven-jeweled flowers to the Buddha; suspended in the void, they formed a floral canopy.
Its light universally illumined the lands of the ten directions, as the multitudes gathered to receive his Dharma teachings.
The Holy One’s virtue is like Mount Sumeru, and the light of his wisdom surpasses the sun and moon;
that which he expounds is beyond all analogy—therefore, I bow my head to the Great Sage, the Hero.
At that time, after Puming had praised the Buddha with these verses, he knelt with palms joined and asked:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Among those gathered here, some have resolved their minds toward Bodhisattvahood, while others have not yet done so."
There are those who have attained non-retrogression, and those who have not yet attained it;

there are those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and have perfected the virtues of being in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
and there are those who remain bound by the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.

The Tathāgata, out of his profound compassion, has extensively revealed this infinite treasury, causing those who have not yet attained understanding to achieve sudden enlightenment, and allowing the ignorant and darkened to behold the light and attain non-retrogression. Is there indeed a samādhi named "Universal Illumination," which dissolves both the deep and the shallow, enabling one to swiftly reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Samantaprabha!

You have great compassion and bring great peace and security; you take pity on the devas and the people of the ten directions, desiring that each may find their proper place. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!”
“Yes, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“There is a samādhi named ‘Surpassing Solar Radiance. When a bodhisattva attains this, there is nowhere they cannot enter.”

For example, wherever the sunlight appears, it manifests without obstruction; so too, for those who transform the cycle of beginning and end, it causes them to fully express the mental activities of the three realms. For those who have not yet resolved their minds but give rise to the Bodhisattva mind, or who have already resolved their minds toward the Way and reached the stage of non-retrogression, it establishes them in the state of non-regression until they reach the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Having attained this stage of being one birth away, they ultimately realize the unsurpassed, true, and correct path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is equal to empty space—without going or coming, neither emerging nor entering, yet there is nowhere it does not act.
“By practicing eighty matters, one truly attains this samādhi. What are these eighty? One understands that the eye is empty;

one removes attachment to the ear and sounds; there is no smelling by the nose; one uproots clinging to speech; one delivers the consciousness; one ceases lustful desire; one rests from anger and resentment; and one relinquishes ignorance.”
One realizes that form is like foam, sensation is like a bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion;
the mind is fundamentally pure, and the intellect is likened to a dream;

thought is like a reflected image; one does not perceive a body, does not reckon a person, does not possess a life-span, and does not preserve a vital breath; the four great elements are empty, the five aggregates have no root, the six sense-fields have no origin, and the seven consciousnesses have no master.
Practicing a mind of loving-kindness, feeling compassion for all, with a will that is harmonious and joyful, guarding the sense faculties;
being without hatred or attachment, free from all dualities, without distracted conduct, and without association;
there is no giving yet no stinginess, no precepts yet no transgression, no patience yet no anger, no diligence yet no indolence, no tranquility yet no agitation, and no wisdom yet no folly.
Not abandoning the mundane nor being exclusively devoted to the Way;
preaching the Dharma not for oneself but for all beings;
without attachment, yet neither severed nor bound.
Being without conceptual understanding, one practices equanimity;
having cast off sleepiness, one is free from the hindrances;
not being subject to sensory entry, one does not follow after dualistic oppositions; the mind is spontaneously liberated, in accord with the Buddha’s teaching.
Not violating the Dharma, nor disparaging the assembly;
they have compassion for the people of the ten directions, like a father’s strict instruction, like a mother’s nurturing care, and like a child’s obedience toward its parents;
their kindness is as if toward one's own person.
Not acting for the sake of one's own form, nor for the sake of others, nor for the sake of dharmas;
practicing the bodhisattva path with a broad and noble resolve, free from perverse thoughts;
without the notion of a śrāvaka, without the intent of a pratyekabuddha, and seeking no expectations; abandoning the practices of "self" and "other," remaining entirely without dependence.
Not perceiving the three periods of time, one realizes the fundamental nature of the triple world;
not relying on mind, thought, or consciousness, one understands that the Way is like emptiness;
transcending past, future, and present, one enters deeply into great wisdom.
"All things are originally non-existent; one practices great skillful means.
This constitutes the eighty [eighth].
The Buddha said to Puming:
"If one follows and cultivates these eighty practices, one will swiftly attain the Samādhi of Surpassing Solar Radiance.
Just as when the sun rises it illuminates everywhere at once, such that the hundred grains, grasses, and trees—all things that look toward the heavens—reach maturity;
so too does one who attains this samādhi equally enter all superior, middling, and inferior modes of practice, manifesting in all places and delivering all beings."
Just as the full moon dispels the deep darkness of night;
so too, by advancing with the light of great meditative concentration, one casts back the obscuration of the three defilements and, having eliminated them, beholds the supreme path.
Just as a great king of physicians selects and gathers a hundred medicines to treat various illnesses, so that each and every one is healed; [so does this practitioner].

With boundless wisdom, he preaches the Dharma according to the fundamental practices of sentient beings, causing them to transcend form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness so that they may attain supernormal powers.
Furthermore, like a boatman steering a sturdy vessel, he ferries people back and forth without hindrance;

he manifests nirvana to save immeasurable beings, transforming them and bringing them to rest, explaining the emptiness of the three realms, and following them from beginning to end to rescue and gather all living creatures.
Just as a majestic lion dwelling in the forests and thickets causes all other beasts to submit and be cowed;

so too does the Bodhisattva who has attained this samādhi walk alone and traverse the three periods of time, subduing and casting aside all those who have fallen into the sixty-two views or the ninety-six paths of heterodoxy, leading them to receive the teachings of the Way and enabling them to find their proper place within the three vehicles.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King governs the four realms and is venerated by all under heaven, so too does this Samādhi employ the four immeasurables through the four modes of mental application;

it analyzes the four great elements to deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, self, person, and life-span, causing them to realize that these are fundamentally non-existent and leading them to the Great Way.
Just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams and contains every kind of treasure, rare and wondrous gem;

so too do all gateways of the Dharma, dhāraṇīs, eloquence, and doors of meditative concentration all converge therein. It radiates the profound meaning of unsurpassed wisdom, causes the Three Jewels to flourish, washes away ignorance and darkness, and transcends to the sublime samādhi of the Sun-Light.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Just as when the sun rises, Its light shines everywhere;
The hundred grains look up and ripen— Great Samādhi surpasses even that."
Reaching equality with all beings, including those of diverse natures and various classes of living creatures;
he manifests everywhere without exception, so that none fail to attain transcendence.
Like a King of Physicians who cures all ailments, he administers medicine according to the time.
This samādhi is truly appropriate; it eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.
Like a ferryman who carries people back and forth, one travels from this shore to the other;
so too is the Bodhisattva, whose saving of beings is without end.
Just as a majestic lion strides alone without fear,
so too are these sixty-two views of doubt all subdued and transformed by this samādhi.
Like a Wheel-Turning Sage King who brings peace and relief to the four continents, [the Tathāgata] likewise pacifies the world.
The Bodhisattva is just like this, Delivering the multitudes through the four immeasurables.
As the great ocean receives the myriad rivers And their rare, exquisite, and wondrous treasures;
So does this samādhi encompass all dharmas, Bestowing the seven kinds of great wealth.
"If there should be one who resolves their mind, desiring to reach unsurpassed wisdom, they should honor this definitive meaning;
thus they shall swiftly attain true and perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha spoke to Puming:
“Bodhisattvas have four matters by which they swiftly attain this samādhi.
What are the four?

They pity the masses of beings as if they were their own marrow and bones; they plant the roots of all virtues without hoping for their reward; they contemplate the four great elements as empty, like a dream; and they reckon the five aggregates as being fundamentally like a mirage.”
"These are the four matters.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One who wishes to attain a concentrated mind Should have compassion for the classes of sentient beings;
Just as one’s own marrow and bones, one establishes virtue without thinking of recompense.
Contemplating that the four elements of the body are empty, it is as fleeting as a dream;
reckoning that the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent, they are like a mirage in the wild.
"If one possesses liberating wisdom, one does not conceive of a self;
by thoroughly investigating the source of all things, one swiftly attains this state of meditative concentration.
The Buddha told Puming:
"Bodhisattvas have four qualities by which they swiftly attain this samādhi.
What are the four?

They nurture all sentient beings with love as if for their own infants; they constantly practice great compassion without distinction between self and other; they exhort the ignorant and show them the light of the Way; and they are diligent day and night, setting their will upon the Way without seeking anything else."
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Protecting and cherishing sentient beings with compassion, Just as parents love their children;"
Great compassion does not weary in its hope; with an impartial mind, it knows neither partiality nor aversion.
It exhorts and guides the ignorant and dull-witted, causing them to behold the brilliance of the Great Way.
Delighting in the True Dharma day and night, one is then able to attain this samādhi.
The Buddha told Puming:
"A bodhisattva has six matters by which they quickly attain this samādhi.
What are the six?

Practicing giving with equanimity; upholding the precepts without any transgression; donning the armor of the Mahāyāna through the power of patience; diligently cultivating vigor without ever becoming lax or negligent; concentrating the mind with single-minded focus so that no manifold thoughts arise; and possessing clear wisdom that does not cling to the triple world—these are the six.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Practicing generosity without expectation, Guarding the precepts like a mountain or the earth;
Establishing the great power of patience— This is donning the armor of the Mahāyāna."
He has well cultivated great diligence, never having known weariness or rest;
with a single mind in dhyāna-samādhi, his wisdom is without obstruction.
He does not perceive the transformations of conditions, nor that from which they arise and are established.
"The three realms suddenly appear and vanish; the single mind dwells nowhere.
The Buddha told Puming:
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi."

What are these ten? They are: bestowing peace and security upon others; eliminating all defilements and harms; dissolving worldly afflictions (*kleśa*); reconciling those who are separated; releasing and resolving the sixty-two types of false views and doubts; understanding the non-existence of a self (*anātman*); constantly honoring the ten virtues; desiring to rescue all beings from the perils of the three miserable realms; not being deluded by the nets of petty arts; and following the primordial non-teaching that is neither joined nor dispersed. These are the ten matters.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Bestowing peace and joy upon sentient beings, Freeing them from all notions of defilement and harm;
Dissolving the dust of worldly toil, Reconciling those who are scattered and estranged."
He explains the sixty-two views, clearly understanding that there is no self;
he constantly honors the ten virtues, desiring to rescue and deliver those in the three realms of existence.
He takes pity on all those in the eight difficult states and those who wander through the cycle of birth and death.
Like those who are blind and sightless, they do not realize their own sinking into darkness.
For this reason, great compassion arises, rescuing and liberating them from all perils;
through discerning profound and far-reaching wisdom, one swiftly attains this concentrated mind.
The Buddha told Puming:
"A bodhisattva has seven matters by which they swiftly attain this samādhi.
What are the seven?

To focus the mind exclusively on the Way without other thoughts; to attain mastery over the Dharma and discern its sublime excellence; to maintain a joyful countenance while observing all sentient beings; to know with faith that all phenomena have no fundamental origin; to always exert diligent effort without abandoning the Way; to establish a great resolve for eternal peace;
and to follow and protect the Dharma until attaining Great Samādhi—these are the seven matters.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Exert the mind and focus it single-mindedly on the Path, Never giving rise to other thoughts;
Discerning that all is fundamentally empty, One faces all beings with a serene countenance.”
Having realized the three gates of liberation, one understands that all phenomena are rootless;
constantly practicing diligence, one does not abandon the Way and its teachings.
Establishing a great and expansive resolve, one nurtures oneself until reaching eternal peace.
"Rescuing and protecting those who are deluded, they attain the Sun-Luminosity Samādhi.
The Buddha told Puming:
"A bodhisattva has ten dharmas by which they quickly attain this samādhi."
What are these ten? They are:

no self, no person, no life-span, no vital principle; no śrāvaka, no pratyekabuddha; not abiding in dualistic dharmas; not clinging to the bodhisattva; not conceiving of or seeing a Buddha; not remaining in saṃsāra;
and not abiding in nirvāṇa. These are the ten.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Not perceiving self, person, or individual, Not reckoning body, life, or duration;
Without the mind of a śrāvaka, Having eliminated the notion of a pratyekabuddha."
There are two ways of not abiding in phenomena: the Bodhisattva is without attachment;
they do not conceptualize or perceive a Buddha-body, nor do they dwell in the extremes of existence or non-existence.
Suddenly, without seeing themselves, they perceive that all things are empty.
"When causes and conditions no longer arise, one then attains the concentrated mind.
The Buddha told Puming:
"A bodhisattva possesses eight dharmas by which they swiftly attain this samādhi."

What are these eight? They are: observing the heterodox and the orthodox with equanimity, without dualistic thought; constantly recollecting the Triple Gem so that it is never interrupted; expounding the profound meaning of the Dharma without ever engaging in idle chatter; practicing according to the Mahāyāna and not delighting in the deeds of the disciples; following the Dharma while not abandoning the Buddha-way; employing impartial skillful means to eliminate all arising and ceasing; ensuring that the perception of causes and conditions is forever extinguished; maintaining the tranquility of the mind-cessation (śamatha) without distraction; and, with a single-minded concentration, beholding the ten directions. These are the eight.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Equally observing both the heterodox and the orthodox, neither has any place of abiding;
constantly mindful of the Triple Gem, one causes wisdom never to be severed.”
He expounds the essential points of the profound meaning, never giving rise to thoughts of self-aggrandizement;
he employs his karma to serve the Mahāyāna, having no longing for the Hīnayāna.
His actions always accord with the Dharma, and he does not abandon the Buddha’s true path.
Through the practice of skillful means, one attains equanimity, eliminating all conditions for arising and ceasing.
When the applications of mindfulness reach profound stillness, mental agitation never arises;
with a single mind maintaining meditative concentration, one clearly beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Buddha told Puming:
"There are seven matters by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi.
What are the seven? "

To understand that form is fundamentally empty; that sound is like an echo; that fragrance is like the wind; that taste arises from the conjunction of conditions; that tactile sensation has no true pleasure; and to realize that consciousness is like an illusion and all phenomena are like dreams—these are the seven.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Understand that the essence of form is empty; Sounds heard by the ear are like echoes.
Odors of the nose are like the wind; Tactile sensations are even more fleeting.”
"Having realized that all consciousnesses are illusory transformations, one understands that all phenomena are but dreams;
being able to discern in this way, one attains the Samādhi of Sun-like Radiance.
The Buddha told Puming:
“A bodhisattva has five things by which they swiftly attain this samādhi. What are the five?

They maintain an impartial mind toward people and non-people of the ten directions; they remain free from attachment or aversion regarding offerings and benefits; if there is an exposition of the sutras, they do not fail to proclaim it; they do not look for the treasures of others’ wealth or beauty; and they enter deeply into the subtle, wondrous, and ineffable Dharma.”
"These are the five.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"With an impartial mind toward the ten directions, / There is no distinction between humans and non-humans."
If one receives offerings, one’s resolve remains free from attachment or aversion.
Even if one preaches the sutras, one does not complain of deficiencies even unto death;
having no expectation for the wealth or profit of others, one enters deeply and attains meditative concentration.
The Buddha told Puming:
"There are five things by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi.
What are the five?

Transcending emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness regarding all dharmas; being enlightened in the three types of penetrating knowledge; possessing unimpeded eloquence; practicing the perfection of great wisdom to reach the ultimate; and employing skillful means such that there is nowhere they do not enter—these are the five.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Transcending emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, He has clearly realized the wisdom of the three types of omniscience;
His eloquence is immeasurable, And his teachings are like the great ocean."
"Cultivating great wisdom, that which is delivered is infinite;
skillful means are all-encompassing—the clarity of the sun and meditative concentration are thus!

When the Buddha spoke these words, three billion bodhisattvas all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); thirty thousand people were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and eight thousand bhikṣus reached the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and attained liberation of mind.

The three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways; the heavens rained down flowers and incense; lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; birds and beasts all came together to listen; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions naturally flew there, each holding various flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru to scatter over the Buddha, and offering various kinds of garments, robes, and precious jewels to the World-Honored One.
"A Great Sage is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower, appearing only once in a great while; this Dharma is rare and difficult to meet!

The Buddha’s great supernormal powers have been cultivated through countless kalpas, accumulating merit and expanding his vast compassion. His generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, wisdom, and skillful means were all for the sake of the common people; he has naturally attained these, and his efforts have not been in vain."
I have attained a wholesome benefit in being able to behold the Tathāgata and hear the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Sun-Transcending Samādhi.
How joyful! How joyful!
How could my good fortune have reached such a state?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"It is exactly as you have said; in truth, there is neither one nor many.

Those who believe in the profound Dharma and are able to practice it according to its principles shall attain the ten virtues of wisdom through the *Sūryavairocana-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Transcendent Solar Radiance)."

What are these ten? They are: being fully endowed with the four immeasurables; never tiring of the four ways of attracting beings; revering and honoring great wisdom; universally manifesting great meditative concentration and attaining mastery of supernormal powers;

accomplishing the six perfections and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; possessing skillful means and expedient methods; beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions; being able to govern buddha-lands; being in the stage of "one birth remaining" before Buddhahood; and having already reached the site of enlightenment with the threefold knowledge.
"These are the ten.

When these words were spoken, countless bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and an incalculable number of people resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalanetra who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called the training of a bodhisattva?
What is called the training of a śrāvaka?"
“What is meant by the training of a pratyekabuddha?
The Buddha said:
“To have a mind that is limitless, unimpeded, and serene—this is the training of a bodhisattva.”
To have a limited and obstructed mind that is narrow and biased is the study of the Śrāvakas;
to yearn for the Mahāyāna yet lack wisdom in advancing or retreating, with the mind remaining stagnant in the middle, is the study of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Vimalanetra asked again:
"What is meant by 'the infinite'?
What is meant by 'the unimpeded'?"
"What is meant by 'serene composure'?

The Buddha said, "It is to give rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment; to feel compassion for all beings; and to desire to deliver all classes of creatures, whether crawling, breathing, or sentient."

Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, wisdom, and skillful means, one acts solely for the sake of all beings without regard for one’s own person. One accords with the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and further applies the four ways of attracting others through benevolent giving, kindness, and affection. One benefits others as one would benefit oneself, rescuing and relieving all; transforming those in peril, distress, or poverty into followers of the Way, this constitutes the path of the bodhisattva who trains in wisdom.

Reflect upon one's own faults without scrutinizing the deficiencies of others; revere them as one does one’s parents, as one does a child, or as one does one’s own body, regarding them all as equal and without distinction. Respect all people as one respects those with virtuous qualities; pity all people as one would care for a beloved child. Regard enemies and friends with a mind free from partiality. Understand that the body is empty and sentient beings have no fixed location; that the self is naturally so, and all phenomena are naturally so; that the Way (Dharma) is naturally so, and the Buddha-Dharma is naturally so. All things are fundamentally non-existent, without form and without appearance—this is what is meant by the "limitless."
"In the very source of birth and death, one seeks nirvana but does not see it;
in the very source of nirvana, one seeks birth and death but perceives nothing therein.

One does not loathe birth and death, nor does one dwell in nirvana; one dwells in non-dwelling. It is like the light of the sun, which shines everywhere and reaches all places, yet has no coming or going, and the light itself is without conceptualization."
In this way, the Bodhisattva universally enters into all things yet has nothing to enter; there is also no thought of coming and going or circling about.

It is like the great ocean which contains the seven-jeweled moon-bright pearl; dragons, spirits, crocodiles, snakes, turtles, fish, and tortoises all dwell within it without it increasing or decreasing, and its water is of a single flavor that cannot be defiled.

In this way, the Bodhisattva manifests within the hardships of the three realms of birth and death, yet even when reaching the realm of nirvana and the unconditioned, his mind never increases or decreases, remaining like a bright pearl.

If one is likened to pure water that never becomes turbid, universally delivering all sentient beings into the equal flavor of the various supernormal powers and wisdoms; this is shown to sentient beings as being like medicinal trees and poisonous trees arising within space: while those poisonous trees do not harm the void, those medicinal trees have nothing to treat.

In this way, the bodhisattva, even while amidst the three poisons within the cycle of birth and death, remains unstained; yet, even when situated in the pure realm of nirvana, there is nothing further to purify. He delivers all sentient beings without exception, and though it is said that he "enters," there is in truth no entering, exiting, coming, going, or circling about—this is called non-obstruction.

"The mind of the Way is infinite and has no location; it is neither person nor mind, and is likewise unattainable. The suchness of the mind that delivers sentient beings is the suchness of all dharmas. Those who proceed toward this proceed toward equality; those who proceed toward equality realize perfect enlightenment, in which the three realms do not exist."

There is no stage of the śrāvaka, no station of the pratyekabuddha, and no dwelling of the bodhisattva; one does not abide in the conditioned nor in the unconditioned; there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor any station of the past, future, or present.

There is no one to be delivered, nor is there any being to be born; the fruit of the path is fundamentally non-existent, as are the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; pratyekabuddhahood is fundamentally non-existent, as are the three realms, sentient beings, and the Buddha-way—all these are fundamentally non-existent. This fundamental non-existence is itself true fundamental non-existence; it is without preference or aversion—this is called the mind being serene and at ease.
Vimalanetra asked again:
"What is meant by 'limitation,' and what is meant by 'obstruction'?"
"What is meant by having a narrow and biased mind? The Buddha said:

"It is to fear and loathe the afflictions of birth and death within the three realms, declaring that *nirvāṇa* alone is supreme; to fail to understand the spontaneity of reality; to feel aversion toward the suffering of the body; and to dread wandering through the dust and toil of countless eons. It is to practice giving, observing precepts, patience, single-mindedness, diligence, and the study of wisdom without weariness, bestowing one's head, eyes, ears, nose, marrow, brain, flesh, and limbs as offerings wherever required, beyond all measure."

If one has already attained the state of a Buddha yet harbors this mind in advance, thereby ceasing to study the Dharma of a Bodhisattva and desiring the extinction of the body, this is called "limitation.

Furthermore, having already attained Arhatship, if one wishes to deliver others but perceives the minds of others only through samādhi and dhyāna-concentration, unable to foresee the fundamental roots of all beings in advance; if one does not administer medicine according to the illness but merely desires to dwell long in the world; if one contemplates the foul and impure body as something unpleasant, viewing it like an enemy, a viper, or poison, and seeks to realize nirvāṇa prematurely—this is called "obstruction."

"To abide in nirvāṇa while favoring light and disliking darkness, failing to understand that all phenomena are fundamentally without root, and seeking a place of rest without knowing the wisdom of emptiness—this is called a mind that is biased and narrow."
Vimalanetra again asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'standing in the middle'?
The Buddha said:

"To give rise to the bodhicitta, yet to practice giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom as mere conceptualizations; to desire to obtain the World-Honored One’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his majestic spiritual power, and his holy virtues so that he may stand out from the masses; to fail to understand that the Tathāgata’s transformation is fundamentally non-existent, and instead manifests a physical body and life while erroneously seeking it as if it were real."

Furthermore, it is said that there are those who wish to deliver themselves from the notion of a self, yet do not know that it is fundamentally empty; they practice the four immeasurable minds and the four acts of kindness, but remain attached to their practice until they reach emptiness and abide in the cause of non-seeing and the unconditioned. Not knowing when to advance or retreat, and lacking the wisdom of emptiness, they wish to deliver sentient beings but lack the skillful means and the illumination of the Dharma-body necessary to save them—this is called the study of the Pratyekabuddhas.
When these words were spoken, countless devas and humans all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

Thereupon, the son of a householder named Viśuddhaśāsana, accompanied by five thousand followers, approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“These followers of mine delight in the Buddha-dharma and have all resolved to attain the Way. By accumulating what practices can they reach the wisdom of the Way?”
"What dharma should one practice to attain the gathering of a Buddha-land?
The Buddha said:
"There is one dharma-practice that accords with the intent of the Way."
“What is the one? “The nature of the mind is pliant and supple, directed equally toward all; this is the one.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The nature of the mind is always harmonious and supple; the will is not coarse or wild.
To impartially embrace all beings—this accords with the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that constitute the conduct of a bodhisattva.
What are the two? They are:
a tranquil and pure mind that is free from all attachments and observations; and beholding the non-visible while setting one's will solely upon the Great Way.
These are the two.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The mind pure and ever tranquil, Free from views and all attachments;
Having resolved the sixty-two doubts, One contemplates only the practice of the Great Way.”
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva. What are these three?
Understanding emptiness without attachment, non-characteristic without bondage, and wishlessness without liberation; [these are the three]."
"These are the three.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The mind always clearly understands emptiness; Being signless, it is no longer bound."
"Being wishless and having nothing to be liberated from, one then unties the fetters of the triple world.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
What are these four?"

They constantly observe a mind of loving-kindness, harboring no intent to harm; they nurture the transformation of the Way and constantly cultivate compassion, shedding tears of pity for sentient beings suffering the hardships of birth and death.
They constantly maintain a joyful mind with a serene and pleasant countenance, approaching all living beings without feelings of hatred or attachment.

They constantly practice the mind of protection, exhorting and instructing sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration for the Way, and once that aspiration has been aroused, leading them to the stage of non-retrogression.
"Having become non-retrogressive, one proceeds to the site of enlightenment toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
these are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always following the four immeasurable minds, with a serene countenance and a joyful will;
Compassionately pitying the various classes of sentient beings, shedding tears of sympathetic grief.
Desiring in heart to deliver all beings, maintaining an impartial mind free from both hatred and love."
To provide protection through the Dharma is to accord with the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that constitute the conduct of a bodhisattva.
What are these five?

To uphold the prohibitive precepts without transgression; to concentrate the mind and restrain the will so that the heart becomes tranquil; to understand emptiness through wisdom such that nothing arises; to be liberated from the five aggregates so they have no locus; and to manifest within the triple world while perceiving it as non-existent—these are the five.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Maintaining the precepts without transgression, With samādhi, the mind undisturbed;
Through wisdom, discerning emptiness, One delivers and liberates the aggregate of the five skandhas.”
Beholding the calamities of the three periods of time, they manifest within them;
according to the occasion, they provide instruction and transformation, causing each to attain their proper place.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
What are the six? The eyes behold all as empty; the ears hear no sound; the nose smells no fragrance; the mouth speaks no word; the body perceives no subtle touch;
the mind has no thoughts. These are the six.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"What the eyes behold is entirely empty; What the ears hear is without sound.
In the fragrance of the nose there is no attachment; What exists in the flavors of the tongue?"
"Discerning that the body consists of nothing but the four great elements, and realizing that the mind is fundamentally empty of objective reality;
thus understanding the formless, one then accords with the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that constitute the conduct of a bodhisattva."
What are the seven? They are:
restraint of body, speech, and mind; tranquility; composure; freedom from distraction; and being free from further transgression.
These are the seven.
The Buddha then spoke in verse: "Always restrain one's own body and speech, And keep the mind tranquil and undisturbed;
Through the stillness of samādhi, One attains supernatural powers without exception."
“Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
What are these eight? They are:

the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of skillful means, and the accomplishment of the practice of knowledge.”
"These are the eight.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The perfection of giving, the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, and meditation;"
Wisdom is spontaneously attained; the clarity of the Way is the most honored.
Furthermore, there are nine dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
What are these nine?

To eliminate the five aggregates, remove the six sense-decays, extinguish the three impurities, and clear away the eight difficulties; not to be attached to the triple world, not to yearn for the three periods of time, to leave behind the mind of an arhat, to distance oneself from the thought of a pratyekabuddha, and to always set one’s resolve upon the Great Way—this is the ninth.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Having eliminated the five aggregates and the six sense-fields, Free from the three stains and the eight difficulties;
Not clinging to the triple world, One has no dwelling place throughout the three periods of time."
"Because they are free from the mind of an arhat and lack the thought of a pratyekabuddha,
always aspiring to seek the Great Way— this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that constitute the practice of a bodhisattva."
What are the ten? They are:

the Samādhi of the Dharma Jewel, the Samādhi of Abiding Well, the Samādhi of Immovability, the Samādhi of Transcending Non-turning, the Samādhi of Jewel-Heap Flower, the Samādhi of Sunlight Radiance, the Samādhi of All Beneficial Meanings, the Samādhi of the Present, the Samādhi of Wisdom Light Radiance, the Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation, and the Samādhi of Surpassing Solar Brilliance;
these are the ten.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"By means of the Dharma-jewel samādhi, One dwells well and remains unmoved;
Standing firm and unshakable, This is the Jewel-Heap Flower Samādhi."
Illuminating all benefits and meanings, the light of wisdom shines in the present;
through the samādhi of courageous subduing, one attains a brilliance that surpasses the sun.
Furthermore, Vimalanetra!
When a Bodhisattva practices giving, gods and humans joyfully follow; he transforms those who are stingy so that they have nothing left to begrudge.
When a Bodhisattva observes the precepts, gods and humans joyfully follow; he transforms those who are licentious so that they are free from calamity and transgression.
When a Bodhisattva practices patience, gods and humans joyfully comply; he transforms those who are wrathful and narrow-minded so that not even a trace of resentment remains.
The diligence of the Bodhisattva is what gods and humans delight in following; he transforms those who are indolent and negligent, causing them to establish diligent effort.
The single-mindedness of the Bodhisattva is what gods and humans delight in practicing; he transforms those who are distracted and agitated, causing them to resolve upon peaceful stillness.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is what gods and humans delight in complying with; he transforms those who are obscured and hindered, causing them to penetrate the sacred model.
When the Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), gods and humans rejoice; he transforms those who are unkind, causing them to feel equal compassion and affection.
When the Bodhisattva practices compassion (*karuṇā*), gods and humans rejoice; he transforms the ignorant and deluded, leading them to pity all sentient beings.

When the Bodhisattva experiences joy (*muditā*), gods and humans follow with delight; he transforms those who are sorrowful and distressed, providing them with the self-entertainment of the Dharma drum.
When Bodhisattvas practice protection, devas and humans rejoice in it; they rescue and transform those without support and nurture all beings.
When Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, devas and humans rejoice in listening to it; they transform those whose wills are set on the mundane so that they long for the sacred scriptures.
When Bodhisattvas undergo humble hardships, devas and humans rejoice in showing them respect; they transform those who are arrogant so that they honor and revere the Triple Gem.
The Bodhisattva benefits others; gods and humans delight in their benevolence, transforming those who lack righteousness so that they universally bestow grace.
The Bodhisattva practices equanimity; gods and humans delight in their participation, transforming those who lack magnanimity so that they reach out to those who have not yet attained.

"When Bodhisattvas exercise skillful means (*upāya*), they gather in all sentient beings and transform them into goodness, leading them to achieve equal enlightenment and be born entirely in that land;

when Bodhisattvas practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) to gather in sentient beings—namely, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—they gather in sentient beings and cause them to become tranquil, so that when they attain Buddhahood, all shall be born in that land;

when Bodhisattvas reside in great assemblies and preach the profound and wondrous Dharma, desiring to cause even the crawling insects to receive transcendence and salvation, so that when they attain Buddhahood, all shall be born in that land."
The Bodhisattva practices ten virtues to gather in sentient beings, fully transforming them and protecting their body, speech, and mind;

the Bodhisattva preaches the sutras to eliminate the eight difficulties, gathering in sentient beings so they practice the Eightfold Noble Path, such that when he attains Buddhahood, they shall all be born in his land;

the Bodhisattva examines himself and does not seek out the faults of others, gathering in sentient beings so they leave behind all false views and the sixty-two nets of delusion, such that when he attains Buddhahood, they shall all be born in his land.

The Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to gather in sentient beings, liberating them from the eight fetters so that they may attain the eight emancipations; when he attains Buddhahood, they shall all be born in his land.
The Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to eliminate the eight inconceivables, leading them to the ocean of the inconceivable Dharma-gate; when he attains Buddhahood, they shall all be born in his land.

When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, even if they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they fulfill the Buddha-work by manifesting parinirvāṇa, delivering immeasurable beings so that all may attain the Way.
"Thus it is, Vimalanetra!
Such are the beginning and end of the bodhisattva’s practice.
By responding to this practice, his name is established spontaneously; he brings forth a buddha-land and delivers all sentient beings."

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the elder’s son Vimalanetra and his five thousand attendants all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and they immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, a householder named Jianzheng came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have long heard of the Buddha and have constantly yearned to pay my respects; however, due to the obscuration of my transgressions, I was unable to come myself. Today my wish has finally been fulfilled, and my joy is beyond measure. I shall gaze upon the Honored One without weariness and listen to the Dharma without fatigue. I only pray that you will grant me great grace, so that in every lifetime I may encounter the World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
There are four things by which one is never separated from the Buddha.”
What are these four?

Constantly recollecting the Tathāgata and establishing images of the Buddha; hearing the profound meaning of the sutras and faithfully practicing them; although not seeing the Buddha, clearly understanding that he is fundamentally non-existent; and knowing that the Buddhas of the ten directions are but a single Dharma-body.
These are the four matters by which one does not depart from the Buddhas.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which one, though facing the Buddha in person, does not truly see him. These are:
when the Tathāgata is present, one does not go to listen to the sūtras; one does not grasp their meaning; one is unable to practice them or proclaim them to others.
These are the four ways in which one, though seeing the Buddha face-to-face, is as if not seeing him.”
Furthermore, there are those who see the Buddha and yet conceive of a self; failing to understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, they fall into the four inversions.
Listening to the sutras, they become attached to the sounds and cannot distinguish them from the echoes of their own voices; for such persons, there is no nirvana.

Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and no longer appears in the world, those who hear this sutra will have their minds opened with joy, as if seeing light in the darkness. They will clearly understand that the Tathāgata manifests transformations in accordance with worldly conventions; they will uphold the prohibitions of the Path without contravening the scriptures, abandon the sixty-two heterodox views of external teachings, and practice the four immeasurable minds without hatred or attachment.
Though the Buddha has passed into extinction, one whose resolve reaches such a state will always see him.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'seeing the Buddha,' and what is meant by 'hearing the Dharma'?"
"For what reason do you make this offering?

The Buddha said, "Having beheld the body of the Tathāgata, I contemplate and know that by practicing which deeds one may attain Buddhahood; fundamentally, it is due to the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā)."
To have compassion for all beings as one does for a father, a mother, a child, or one’s own body, and not to crave the four great elements—this is to see the Buddha.

To hear the preaching of the Dharma without clinging to the sounds, but taking up only the Dharma and not the person; to take up the essential meaning rather than the voice, to take up wisdom rather than form, and to take up the truth rather than the words—this is to hear the sutras.

If one sees those who have entered the path—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, or the bodhisattva—one should make offerings with an impartial mind, being humble, submissive, and compliant, without arrogance, in order to behold the assembly of noble ones.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the work of Māra'?
The Buddha said:
"Māra has four matters. What are these four? The first is called the Māra of the body:
the body commits manifold evils, the five aggregates and the six decays do not accord with the Buddha-dharma."
The second is the demon of sensual desires (*kāma-māra*), whose passionate states of craving never cease.
The third is the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), which gives rise to various conceptual attachments and prevents the arousal of mindfulness of the Dharma.

The fourth is the celestial Māra and his retinue, who come to test and beg for offerings without ever being satisfied; yet through the application of mindfulness and the abandonment of unwholesome states, Māra is subdued.

It is like two pieces of wood rubbed together that spontaneously produce fire which then burns the wood itself; this fire does not emerge from water, nor from wind, nor from earth. These four Māras are likewise thus: they all arise from the mind and do not come from without.
For example, it is like a painter creating an image; its size follows the hand.
Although the causes and conditions are assembled—there being pigment, a board, and a brush—if the painter does not paint, the image cannot be formed.
The four māras are thus: when the mind is already firm and nothing arises, then there are no four māras.

Why is this? Because the five aggregates have no location, the four great elements are fundamentally non-existent, and the twelve links of dependent origination have no beginning; to understand them in this way is to be free from the works of Māra.
"To calculate self, person, or life-span is to fall into the bonds of Māra’s views;
by discerning that there is no body, one subdues Māra.
Viimalanetra addressed the Buddha:
"What is called the Dharma-Jewel Samādhi?
The Buddha said:
"It is the non-interruption of the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
“What is meant by ‘non-interruption’? “It is to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;

to establish the roots of all virtues like Mount Sumeru; to have faith and delight in the Mahāyāna so that the mind does not waver; to first behold auspicious omens in three thousand buddha-fields; to fully possess hundreds of thousands of millions of treasuries; to attain the preeminent and invincible dhāraṇī; and to achieve perfection in the pāramitā of giving.”

At the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one relinquishes the peace of the body and constantly concerns oneself with all beings; one does not regard the pleasures that others delight in as true pleasure, but discards what the world admires and takes the Dharma as one’s joy.
"What is meant by worldly pleasures? "The notions of self, person, and life-span;

the five aggregates and the six sense-fields; the twelve links of dependent origination; music, dance, food, and drink; official rank and emoluments; wealth, property, and nobility; wife, children, slaves, and servants; retinues and attendants; fields, houses, oxen, horses, and carriages—these are the pleasures of the world."

“What is called the joy of the Dharma? It is to clearly understand that there is no self, no person, no life-span, and no soul; to possess the five supernormal powers and the six penetrations; to lecture upon, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the bodhisattva path; never to grow weary of the seven riches of the Dharma; to practice the four debts of gratitude and the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; to perform the myriad virtuous deeds of the six perfections; to harbor no heart of malice or harm; to regard all classes of beings—whether crawling insects, breathing creatures, humans, or spirits—as one’s own realm; not to praise oneself nor disparage others; and for one’s mind to be earnestly and constantly intent upon all things. When gods, dragons, ghosts, and people, great and small, behold such a person, there are none who do not resolve to cultivate virtuous merit. This is called the joy of the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, there are ten practices to be performed. What are these ten? Taking the faculty of faith as foremost;

taking the faculty of concentration as the foundation; taking great loving-kindness as the source; taking great compassion as the honor; making one's will and nature harmonious and gentle; keeping the various supernormal powers and wisdom correct; establishing all sentient beings; taking the four debts of gratitude as primary; regarding the factors of enlightenment as supreme; and vowing to protect the Buddha-dharma as one's own servants."
These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are ten practices that are not transgressed.
What are the ten?

Not killing, stealing, or committing sexual misconduct with the body; not engaging in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech with the mouth; and not harboring ill will, envy, doubt, or wrong views with the mind—these constitute the ten.

“Compassionately regard the ten directions as a mother regards her child; remain undisturbed regarding form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; do not be deluded by worldly people, nor be insulted by worldly glory; do not follow those who are greedy, nor those who are angry, nor those who are ignorant; do not slander the Triple Gem, nor harbor guile; cultivate the six recollections and practice the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, generosity, faith, and wisdom; and in all movements—whether entering or exiting, walking or standing—do not indulge in self-exaltation.”

One who has first resolved their mind is like the moon at its inception, destined to become full; they are seen and protected by devas, nāgas, and spirits, and shall not be harmed by the interference of evil ones.
"To maintain the mind in three dharmas— regarding the Way as a treasure and the world as impermanent— is what is called the Samādhi of the Dharma-Jewel.
Vimalanetra asked again,
"What is meant by the Samādhi of Abiding Well?"
The Buddha said:
"It is like the earth, which receives all things—whether good or evil, beautiful or bitter, fragrant or foul, pure or impure—without being defiled.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: they receive all dharmas and establish themselves through their own cultivation. First, they behold auspicious omens; the three thousandfold world-system is as level as the palm of a hand, adorned with lotus flowers of various jewels. Having attained this supreme and incomparable *dhāraṇī*, they then possess the perfection of transcendent ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)."
"Furthermore, one practices ten things:

eliminating the eight difficult conditions; establishing the virtues of a Buddha; transcending the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; purifying body, speech, and mind; ensuring that all undertakings proceed from the Buddha-dharma; adorning the mental disposition to cross over the calamities of the three miserable realms; fulfilling all vows; and restraining the minds of others. These are the ten."

"In body, they constantly practice loving-kindness; they do not steal nor engage in sexual misconduct. In discussing the sutras and scriptures, they do not pursue superficial elegance. With utmost sincerity, they reconcile disputes; their speech is gentle and never coarse, and they never employ flowery embellishments. They abandon greed and contemplate giving, bringing peace and harmony to others. Free from false views, they delight in the True Dharma."

Constantly contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; regard the world as defiled and take the Dharma as your standard. Cultivate yourself with a mind that is ever-anxious lest you fall short, seeing the body as useless and the five aggregates as detrimental. Seeking to uproot the five desires, hold the Buddha-way as supreme without harboring regret. Observe the impermanence of the heavens and view human beings as like a dream; feeling compassion and pity for those in the three miserable realms who suffer most, by what skillful means shall you deliver yourself from the hardships of birth-and-death and the five aggregates, and transform others as well?
To reckon all people of the ten directions as my own is because I desire to deliver and liberate them. Why is this so?
Because I desire to deliver and liberate them.

When seeing those who come to invade, one does not dwell on their evil; when encountering those who bring light and benefit, one does not dwell exclusively on their goodness. When seeing those who revile, one remains silent and does not retaliate; when struck or beaten, one accepts it without resentment. Toward those who are angry, one directs a heart of loving-kindness; toward those who slight or disparage, one feels compassion and does no harm.

Furthermore, he feels shame for himself, thinking: "For incalculable kalpas, I have remained within birth and death, shrouded by the five aggregates and unable to extricate myself; my mind is deluded and my thoughts confused as they flow through the five rivers, and I have been unable to awaken to the afflictions of the four fears."

There is one who is able to practice giving, knowing that wealth is impermanent and that the body is not "mine. They seek out virtuous friends and distance themselves from evil companions; they direct their intentions toward the Buddha and constantly seek the sublime sutras. They do not crave worldly fame but always act with reverence; they are resolved upon the path of faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and they do not, out of doubt, confusion, violation of prohibitions, indolence, stinginess, or ignorance, abandon the principles of the Way.

"Constantly contemplate the Dharma as one who, hungry, seeks food; gradually enter the Path as a spring flowing afar that eventually enters the sea; and nourish it like a mother who suckles and raises her child."

In managing one’s livelihood and saving lives, one does not engage in hoarding; rather, one provides for one’s parents, brothers, wife, children, slaves, guests, and servants, always mindful of them with compassion and pity, desiring to lead them across [to liberation], so that they do not fall into the three miserable realms but transcend the triple world. Taking refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—one attains the three types of penetrating knowledge and unimpeded wisdom, remaining unstained by the three defilements. One who practices in this manner is well-established in samādhi.
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the Immovable Samādhi?
The Buddha replied:

"Just as the lion, the king of all deer, causes the beasts to tremble with fear before his majesty such that none fail to submit, so too, having first beheld auspicious omens throughout the three thousand buddha-fields, manifesting himself as one who wields the five weapons with valor, and attaining the *dhāraṇī* of 'Abiding in Goodness,' he is then endowed with the perfection of transcendent patience."
“Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten? Taking patience as the foundation, taking faith and joy as the power;

teaching all people the profound and wondrous patience of the Dharma; severing and dispersing all fetters; removing the obstacles of desire; having no longing for the source of the body; not begrudging one’s life-span; surpassing the three gates of liberation through various supernormal knowledges and wisdom; and contemplating the equality of all phenomena.”
These are the ten.
Guarding body, speech, and mind, one constantly gives rise to causes and conditions through all dharmas.
What is meant by "joy in the Dharma"?

They delight in the Buddha-dharma and do not favor worldly ways; they delight in hearing the sutras and do not dwell on mundane talk; they delight in making offerings to the Sangha and do not join worldly factions; they delight only in the Triple Gem and do not set their minds upon the three defilements; they delight in crossing over the three realms and do not allow themselves to be stained; they delight in contemplating the four elements as earth, water, fire, and wind, and do not calculate "me" or "mine"; they delight in bringing peace to people and things and do not engage in harm; they delight in giving away all they possess and do not practice stinginess; they delight in upholding the prohibitions and precepts and do not violate what they follow; they delight in enduring insults and do not lose the root of virtue; they delight in the power of diligence and do not cultivate the roots of evil; they delight in the single-mindedness of dhyāna and do not harbor distracted thoughts; they delight in profound wisdom and do not succumb to folly or delusion.

They delight in transforming worldly afflictions without being defiled by turbidity; they delight in the purity of the Buddha-lands without wearying of the work of conversion; they delight in adorning the Dharma without engaging in what is non-Dharma; they delight in the three gates of liberation while remaining free from the marks of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they delight in the unconditioned Dharma without delighting in worldly affairs; they delight in entering the profound Dharma without losing their integrity; and their will delights in joy, remaining free from anger and lack of clarity.

One delights in the natural Dharma yet does not abandon sentient beings; one delights in cultivating virtuous friends and distancing oneself from worldly intimacy; one delights in constantly setting the mind on the Path and not creating delusion; one delights in expounding correct discourse and not following secular texts; one delights in admiring Bodhisattvas and not being a Śrāvaka; one delights in seeking perfect enlightenment and not being a Pratyekabuddha; one delights in heading toward the Great Way and not practicing minor arts; one delights in maintaining the Eightfold Equanimity and not practicing the Eightfold Perversions; one delights in the wisdom of the sixty-two [types of] insight and does not fall into the body of the sixty-two views; one delights in the unsurpassed Dharma and does not practice that which is inferior; one delights in the practice of the Mahāyāna and discards the dharma of the Arhat.
This is the joy of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are ten matters by which one quickly attains the awakening of concentration.
What are these ten matters?

To have a compassionate heart that pities others and does no harm; to constantly practice the ten wholesome deeds and remain far removed from evil conduct; to devote oneself single-mindedly to the cultivation of the Way; to contemplate the Buddha and the Dharma with virtuous thoughts as one who seeks food when hungry or drink when thirsty; to universally honor the profound meaning and not allow other thoughts to distract; to maintain compassion for the ten directions; and to desire to deliver all beings without thinking of oneself—these are the ten.

"This is why it is called the Dharma of the Immovable Samādhi: because it transcends the first and second samādhis; because one is not deluded by the dharmas of desire; because one practices the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind; and because through giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, one rescues sentient beings from the hardships of the three evil realms. Gradually cultivating great compassion with the intent to save those in the three worlds, one regards all people as no different from oneself; free from other thoughts, one constantly maintains mindfulness of the Dharma; taking the Dharma as the foundation and worldly affairs as faults, one always pities all living beings, desiring to lead them all to the Way—this is the Immovable Samādhi."
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Transcending the Unshakable'?
The Buddha said:

"It is like a natural hook-locked wrestler of fierce and powerful strength, who opens up many paths, walking alone as a heroic and eminent figure without peer. Having eliminated all defilements, harms, and the enmity of worldly afflictions, he first beholds auspicious omens throughout the three thousandfold Buddha-fields: great winds blow from the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, and various kinds of flowers pervade the Buddha-fields. By attaining the discernment of the unassailable *dhāraṇī*, he then possesses the perfection of transcendent progress."
“Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten?

Taking the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) and the power of diligence (*vīryabala*) as the foundation, and taking equanimity (*samatā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as the primary elements; causing all people not to crave or delight in the body, but instead transforming sentient beings through mind and speech; abiding without regression yet remaining nowhere; possessing supreme diligence that subdues enmity and intimidation; and the diligent cultivation and accomplishment of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).”

These are the ten. One contemplates that the body composed of the four great elements is like a venomous snake; one fears old age, illness, and death, and does not abandon the cycle of beginning and end to engage in deluded affairs. With loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one regards all classes of beings—whether crawling, breathing, or sentient—as equal to a father, a mother, a child, or one’s own body, without distinction. One constantly reflects upon the meaning of the Path, remaining free from greed, anger, and delusion; one contemplates practicing giving and does not harbor thoughts of stinginess;
one upholds the prohibitions and precepts and does not commit acts of evil.
To practice patience with the thought of being free from anger;
to constantly cultivate diligence with the thought of being free from indolence;
and to focus the mind single-mindedly with the thought of being free from distraction.
Practice wisdom correctly, free from thoughts of darkness or obscuration;
constantly seek skillful means with a sincere mind and wise expediency, free from thoughts of negligence.
"In mindfulness, exhort and transform others as if delivering one's own self; regard all that exists as not belonging to a self."

When contemplating those who have fallen into the hells, one regards their suffering of toxic agony as if it were happening to oneself; one constantly reflects upon one’s own faults and takes the burden of their transgressions upon oneself, harboring no resentment.

When contemplating the realm of hungry ghosts, who are destitute with hunger and thirst, one weeps for them, trembling with a heart chilled by fear, desiring to deliver them so that they may naturally attain peace and security. One causes them to partake of the food of the Dharma to eliminate the thirst of the five aggregates and the six decays: reciting and studying the scriptures serves as their meal, discerning the meaning of the sutras serves as their drink, practicing the six dharmas serves as their virtue, and their every movement and step is characterized by diligence and composure.

Reflecting on those who have fallen among the beasts, one should always harbor compassion, desiring to bring them peace and security so they may exhaust their prior debts, bring an end to the sins of past lives, and refrain from creating new ones; one should practice all that is good and commit no evil. Having observed for oneself that throughout successive lifetimes one has failed to achieve liberation—sitting in calculation upon the notion of "self" and failing to believe in the Way and the Dharma—one should consider the offender as if submerged in a deep abyss, while regarding the mind that upholds the Dharma and trusts in the precepts as being like space. Those who do not understand the Dharma transmigrate through the five realms of existence like the turning of a wheel.

Parents worry for one another, brothers think of one another, and husbands and wives long for one another; their resolve is not firm. Those who were once parents become children, and those who were originally children become parents; those who were once spouses become enemies. Thus, the inversion of high and low is the very root of impermanence.

"This Bodhisattva constantly regards them with a compassionate mind, transforming and instructing them so that they may believe and enter the Buddha’s true path; he leads them to faith and understanding that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—this is called the Samādhi of Deliverance through Immovability."
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the Jewel-Heap Flower Samādhi?
The Buddha said:

"It is, for example, like the Pārijāta tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by means of various past practices, one transcends the five faculties, and the purity of the sentient being's mind becomes like space. First, one beholds auspicious omens within the three thousandfold world-systems; amidst the blending of various sounds and music, one adorns one’s body with necklaces and ornaments, while the radiance of the saugandhika flower illuminates one’s form. One rains down flowers of liberation and blue lotuses as they attend upon one from above."
For this reason, the various virtues of total retention (dhāraṇī) constitute the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Furthermore, there are ten matters.
What are these ten?

To subdue the sense faculties as the foundation of virtue, to take single-mindedness as one’s strength, to employ impartial skillful means, to maintain a concentrated mind without distraction, to take the prohibitive precepts as the source, to regard the gates of liberation as supreme, to proceed toward fixed concentration while remaining without grasping, to extinguish and destroy worldly afflictions, and to fully contemplate all states of meditative absorption— these are the ten.

“Compassionately pitying those in the five realms of existence, he attacks and eliminates the five aggregates (*skandhas*), establishes the five faculties (*indriyas*), and purifies the five objects of form (*rūpa*). Having accumulated merit, he is fully endowed with the five categories—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Aspiring to the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the ten powers (*bala*), he shall receive them; he shall never encounter calamities or transgressions. In every place of birth, he will constantly cultivate the Buddha-dharma; his fame and virtue will spread far and wide as he compassionately pities the three realms, and he will not remain deluded, clearly discerning the paths of good and evil.”
Just as the myriad rivers flow toward the four seas and enter the channels of swift water, so too does the practice of this bodhisattva who reveres the Dharma:
through unremitting diligence, he advances toward the Great Way.
Just as when the moon is on its tenth day, its radiance increases and shines upon sentient beings;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, whose merit and majestic brilliance increase day by day, delivering all from peril and distress while taking pity on the sufferings of the masses.
"Furthermore, there are five practices. What are these five?
