One's observance of the five precepts is pure, like a bright mirror free from any stain; one fulfills the ten wholesome actions without transgression; one does not lose the resolve for the Way; one does not harbor perverse thoughts; and one does not covet one's own body."
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are another five:
removing the color of anger, being free from a timid mind, abandoning the intent of stinginess and greed, and eliminating the disposition of flattery and deceit.
Discerning and understanding emptiness, they do not merely speak of it with their mouths but constantly cultivate a single-mindedness free from distracted conduct;

they know that nobility, power, wealth, and pleasure are like illusions, and they contemplate form as a bubble, sensation as foam, perception as a plantain tree, volitional formations as a shadow, and consciousness as a magical display;

they are not driven by form, not deluded by sensation, not turned back by perception, not led astray by volitional formations, and not regressed by consciousness—thus they understand the emptiness of the five aggregates.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are another five.
What are these five?
Greed, lust, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt— having removed these five hindrances,

he possesses the power of clear vision and penetrating hearing, the ability to move with lightness and fly, knowledge of the thoughts in others' minds, and self-knowledge of his own origins and the places of birth and death through which he has passed; thus he enjoys himself by means of the five supernormal powers,
yet does not become negligent on account of the five aggregates.
He cultivates virtuous conduct in his person and refrains from unrighteous acts; he enlightens others through preaching the Dharma, bringing peace and security to many.
He does not engage in manifold evils or harmful deeds, taking the Way as his occupation, practicing the Dharma as his food, and understanding its meaning as his drink.
He does not long for wealth or nobility, regarding the Dharma as his true wealth and the realization of emptiness as his true nobility.
“This is the Jewel-Heap Flower Samādhi.
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is called the Sunlight Radiance Samādhi?”

The Buddha said: "First, one beholds auspicious omens: the sight of three thousand buddha-fields, where bathing pools of various jewels are filled with the eight kinds of excellent water, clear and limpid. They are planted with blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses; their surrounding railings are made entirely of the seven treasures; they are accompanied by auspicious flowers, and their bottoms are spread with golden sand. Therein, one’s own person enjoys and sports."
Upon attaining the concentration of wisdom and realizing the dhāraṇī, one then possesses the transcendent perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten?

Wisdom is the root; the power of wisdom is supreme; right view is the foremost; equanimity of mind is the most excellent. Cultivating the various virtues of the body, one enters entirely into the characteristics of all the noble truths as the characteristic of equality. Wisdom is free from the hindrances of the aggregates, eliminates all past views, and gives rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
These are the ten matters.
"Observe that the six sense-faculties are fundamentally without location; they come from nowhere and go nowhere. They are originally empty by nature, arising only through the encounter of conditions.

For example, rain does not emerge from the dragon, nor from the water, nor from the earth, nor from the dragon’s mind; it is only through the convergence of causes and conditions that this rain is brought forth."
The six sense-faculties and the various bases (āyatana) are likewise so; they are formed through causes and conditions and cannot exist independently, and birth-and-death is just like this.

It is, for example, like a painter who creates images of people, houses and dwellings, elephants, horses, and carriages. Before they have been painted, their location is not seen; yet by skillfully treating the wall-boards with a base coat and then applying brushwork and pigments, and by the gathering and convergence of all these various conditions, they are brought to completion.
Good and evil are thus formed through the convergence of causes and conditions.

Furthermore, if one practices the Way, it is through the ten wholesome actions, the six perfections—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—and skillful means that they are brought together.

They do not cling to the Buddha-body nor do they depart from it; their minds and intentions are free of conceptualization, naturally like space. They gradually enter into great kindness (*maitrī*), further cultivating great compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). They do not act for their own sake but always for the sake of all beings, yet they harbor no seeking. Their physical conduct is prudent and restrained, their speech is humble and compliant, and their mental reflections are gentle and mild; they are without flattery, being simple and upright without guile.
"Furthermore, there are six things by which one swiftly attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

What are these six? Constantly dwelling in reliance upon the Buddha; entering into the true mind so that the heart does not regress; clearly understanding one's own internal mental activities; being entrusted by virtuous friends; having vast and expansive aspirations without weariness or satiety; and having a mind that is not discordant and lacks no wisdom."
This is the sixth.

"When a bodhisattva practices the Way, they do not rely on form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not rely on the internal or external. They follow the teachings of the fundamental Dharma, do not contravene the profound and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva, do not abandon great kindness, and do not lose great compassion, providing relief according to whatever the world lacks."

Cultivating the path with correct transformation and not succumbing to false teachings; directing the single mind toward wisdom and not being obscured by folly; discerning the six decays as being like transformations, illusions, shadows, echoes, heat-mist, the moon in water, or what is seen in a dream—suddenly unknown where it has gone—this is called the Sunlight Radiance Samādhi.
"It greatly moved him and brought about his compliant patience toward the Dharma.
Viśuddhanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the Samādhi that Accomplishes All Beneficial Meanings?"
The Buddha said:

"First, one beholds auspicious omens and sees the three thousand buddha-fields; one observes the bathing pools of various jewels to their left and right; one delivers those in the perils of hell and wanders through the wilderness; and upon attaining the marvelous dhāraṇīs of the gathered assembly, one is fully endowed with the infinite power of transcendent skillful means."
"Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten? Entering into all modes of conduct; establishing sentient beings;

taking infinite great compassion and universal pity as the foundation; having a mind that is harmonious and supple, never becoming weary; relinquishing the vehicles of the disciples and pratyekabuddhas; observing with thorough discernment; guiding others toward the mind of the Way; establishing non-retrogression through various supernormal powers and wisdom; and awakening to vast knowledge."
These are the ten matters.
"Always employing right wisdom, one remains far removed from false views; naturally practicing the Way, one is not deluded by worldly things;
deeply penetrating the subtle and infinite Dharma, one enters universally among both the monastic and the laity, being neither worldly within the secular nor [detached] within the monastic."
Without dependence, one contemplates the holy teachings to transform sentient beings; one constantly guards the body against old age, sickness, and death;
one repels the six sense-faculties so as not to fall into the six degenerations; one does not follow the seven perversions but constantly maintains the seven factors of enlightenment;
with a mind that is not crooked, one’s diligent effort is never abandoned; one accords with the Dharma without opposition, being joyful and free from resentment; and the root of faith is unshakable.
Deluded yet finding peace and security, their will is steadfast and undisturbed; they possess the wealth of faith and the wealth of wisdom as their fundamental nature, and the wealth of precepts.

They do not fall into the Lesser Vehicle, possessing the wealth of shame and remorse; they feel remorse for not having attained deliverance from the three realms, and they feel shame for not expanding their wisdom.
Possessing the wealth of extensive learning, their hearing is peerless; reaching the most profound and far-reaching wisdom, they practice the wealth of giving.
By means of the wealth of the wisdom of the Great Way, one enters into wisdom to universally deliver all beings.
There are ten matters that lead to the stage of non-retrogression.
What are these ten?

Hearing that there is deliverance or no deliverance, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is the Dharma or no Dharma, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is the Sangha or no Sangha, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is the Path or no Path, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there are Bodhisattvas or no Bodhisattvas, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is the Dharmakāya or no Dharmakāya, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is the mundane or the non-mundane, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is a person or no person, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is life or no life, the mind does not waver or turn back; hearing that there is longevity or no longevity, the mind does not waver or turn back. These are the ten.

"Flying to the ten directions to teach and transform the various devas and all living beings, taking the Dharma as the foundation and the Way as the source, they do not reckon in terms of self; sometimes they enter hell to rescue them from suffering and pain;
sometimes they enter the realm of birds and beasts to enlighten and transform ignorance and darkness;
or they enter the realm of hungry ghosts to comfort and satisfy their hunger and venom."
Adapting to worldly customs to instruct and transform beings so that each finds their proper place, yet remaining unstained by worldly dharmas;

pure as the radiance of the sun and brilliant as the fullness of the moon; the Bodhisattva attains non-retrogression and is able to exercise skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); wherever there is need for rescue and salvation, many are protected and delivered; all those suffering from afflictions obtain great peace, and all those lacking wisdom are fully endowed with broad intelligence and strategy—this is the attainment of the Samādhi of All Beneficial Meanings.
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the samādhi of standing before the eyes of all present Buddhas?
The Buddha said:

"It is like when the moon is at its full height, all darkness is dispelled; this is a metaphor for how all that one has cultivated with diligence becomes pure, and all that one aspires to is fulfilled. Having established a Buddha-land and training sentient beings, one first beholds auspicious omens throughout the three thousandfold world-system: a lion, king of deer, wearing a silken cloth upon its head, its body tall and massive, its majestic power subduing the various beasts."
Upon attaining the eighty-four thousand gateways of the infinite *dhāraṇīs*, one is fully endowed with transcendence through the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are ten matters:

first, to fix the mind in meditative concentration for three months, free from discursive thought, single-mindedly directing the will toward the Buddha; to sever all manifold perceptions and not engage in any seeking; to understand that all phenomena are entirely empty; to have no fear of the triple world; to take no pleasure in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); to not calculate the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); and to realize and know the Dharma-body.
These are the ten.

In whichever direction he hears of a presently existing Buddha, he constantly keeps that quarter in mind, beholding the assembly of the fourfold disciples as the Buddha preaches the Dharma to them; he contemplates the emptiness of the four great elements: that earth is like a mass of foam, water is like morning dew, fire is like a flash of red lightning, and wind is like a waving fan.
One discerns that the four great elements arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions and are fundamentally non-existent.
One observes one's own physical form and examines all its roots to find no shape or appearance;
one observes one's own sensations and knows that, fundamentally, there are no sensations.
Observing one's own thoughts, one examines all thoughts and knows that fundamentally there are no thoughts;
observing one's own mind, one knows that fundamentally there is no mind. Through this observation of one's own emptiness, one perceives that all things are non-existent.

"Compassionately pitying those in the eight difficulties, he has relinquished the eight worldly concerns: prosperity and decline, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, and hardship and ease; he has abandoned the eightfold wrong path and does not abide even in the eightfold right path."

Regarding existence or non-existence in such states, there is likewise no abiding; one practices the four immeasurable minds—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and through the four debts of gratitude, rescues the masses by means of generosity, benevolence, benefit, and impartial advantage.

With single-minded devotion toward the Buddha and free from all conceptual thoughts, the five aggregates are severed and the six sense-fields find no footing; the mind thus attains concentration. One does not perceive the four great elements, nor does one see sentient beings; one beholds neither heaven nor earth, nor people or things, seeing nothing at all for a long time, until finally one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions.
It is like turbid water in which the bottom cannot be seen; if it remains still for a long time without movement, it becomes clear and transparent upon close inspection.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: when they have attained concentration and are free from discursive thought, they observe that there is nothing to be seen; the five aggregates and the six sense-decays vanish suddenly like clouds dispersing, and the sun and moon shine forth as they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Observing this further, [he wondered]: "Did I go to where the Buddha was, or did the Buddha come here?
Then his mind reflected: "The Buddha did not come, nor did I go."
For example, when one observes a form in a bright mirror, clear water, or pure oil, the reflection is seen without entering or exiting.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions without coming or going.
It is like a person who, in a dream, returns to their native village and sees their own parents, brothers, wife, and children, yet upon waking finds them nowhere.
So it is with the Bodhisattva: though they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions while in samādhi, upon awakening from that state, they see nothing at all.
Why is this so? Because one understands that they are fundamentally non-existent; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are merely manifestations of transformation!
They have no form and no location.
For example, just as with space, one cannot distinguish or know what specifically constitutes "space," so too is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya):

it has no fixed location, yet it can perceive and penetrate the source of all things. Seated and beholding the ten directions, it neither goes nor comes; this is the Samādhi of the Present Buddhas Standing Before One’s Eyes.
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom?
The Buddha said:

"First, we behold auspicious omens in three thousand Buddha-fields: the Wheel-Turning Sage King establishes the teaching of the Dharma-King, surrounded by immeasurable gentlemen, ministers, and hundreds of thousands of retinues, who hold various precious flowers in the void to cover his body."
Upon attaining the gate of the *dhāraṇī* of inexhaustible practices and the wisdom of six million *koṭis* of *dhāraṇīs*, one is fully equipped to transcendently transform and teach sentient beings.

Just as a divine moon-pearl satisfies the needs of all who are impoverished and destitute, so too does one possess all dharmas to instruct the multitudes, bestowing an inexhaustible treasury of virtue upon all people according to their needs.
“Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten? They are: giving the gift of Dharma;

gathering those who are unruly through the precepts; gathering the violent through patience; gathering the arrogant and indolent through diligence; gathering the distracted through single-mindedness; gathering those with false wisdom through insight; transforming beings according to the times through skillful means and propagating the Great Way by means of the Mahāyāna; roaming among the eight difficulties to escape the eight heterodox practices; and maintaining an impartial mind toward all beings without partiality or bias.”
These are the ten.
"Abiding in the eight inconceivables, one does not forsake the bodhisattva path; one contemplates the three realms as being like illusions and transformations, not regarding them as real.
One reflects for oneself: 'From where do I come, and to where do I go?'"
Without perceiving coming or going, they follow along with moving and staying, each existing as a distinct entity, like a mirage.

In summer, while traveling through a vast wilderness where no people dwell, one sees from afar a great river flowing with water; beside it grow various kinds of trees bearing fruit that are exceedingly lush and flourishing.
That person was hungry and thirsty; having become so exhausted by the heat that it is beyond description, he wished to go toward it.
Looking at it, it seemed close, yet as he ran for several *li*, he could not see the water at all; he then realized it was a mirage and there was no water.
When those who have attained realization see water repeatedly, they know there is no water and do not run toward it in pursuit.

Sentient beings who do not understand that the three realms are like illusions and transformations calculate "self" and "life-span"; yet upon hearing the Buddha preach the sutras on universal impermanence, they awaken to this truth and no longer fall into delusion.

When a bodhisattva understands and realizes that all places within the triple world are like transformations, like illusions, like shadows, like mirages, like dreams, or like the moon reflected in water—knowing them all to be fundamentally non-existent—they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation, seeking nothing at all.
Just as a mother swallow raises her young, so too does the Bodhisattva transform and guide all beings without leaving any behind.
It is like a guide who leads many merchants back to their own hometown; encountering no evil bandits, they arrive home in safety.

In this way, the Bodhisattva, through the concentration of the Samādhi of Radiant Wisdom, leads all beings out of the darkness of the three poisons—lust, anger, and delusion—and reveals the Three Vehicles, with the Mahāyāna as their foundation, so that each may find their proper place.
It is like a king of physicians who, seeing the ailments of the multitude, prescribes medicine according to their specific illnesses, so that none of those afflicted by disease fail to be cured.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva, through the Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom, universally perceives the sufferings of the five destinies and the cruel pains of the three poisons among all sentient beings. With great compassion, he transforms and enlightens them, causing them to uphold the correct teachings and the infinite wisdom. For those who have not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment, he causes them to do so; for those who have already generated it, he strengthens their progress and dedication; and for those who have ascended to the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood," he leads them to the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path. This is the concentration of the Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom.
Vimalanetra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation'?
The Buddha said:

"It is, for example, like a Wheel-Turning Sage King, whose meritorious reign is immeasurable and whose majestic virtue is towering; having attained sovereignty, he has acquired inexhaustible wisdom regarding all phenomena."

Compared to the empty space that is stainless and pure, one first beholds auspicious omens throughout three thousand buddha-fields: the Tathāgata’s form, with a complexion like purple-polished gold, its radiance circular and encompassing countless hundreds of billions of Brahma-virtues as he preaches the sutras; having attained the gate of dharanis for immeasurable practices and hundreds of thousands of koṭis of dharani-practices as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he is fully endowed with transcendent noble wisdom and has accomplished much.

“Furthermore, there are ten matters. What are these ten? They are: to resolve upon omniscience without partiality; to abide neither in the conditioned nor in the unconditioned; to practice universal loving-kindness equally toward all sentient beings; to practice great compassion as vast as space; to have no thought of being a disciple and no notion of being a bodhisattva; to have neither worldly intent nor the aspiration for the Path; to always employ great wisdom to transform the multitudes in accordance with their needs; to enter into all forms of birth yet remain without being born; to manifest in all Buddha-lands without abandoning the Dharma-body; and to maintain an equanimous mind regarding both the self and nirvana.”

These are the ten matters. "He does not engage in any verbal or physical actions; his mind is always stable, neither increasing nor decreasing. Manifesting in the realm of desire, he transcends all sensory dusts; though naturally amidst desires, he has no attachment and seeks nothing at all, like a lotus flower that is unstained by dust or water.

Manifesting in the realm of form, he naturally seeks nothing regarding forms, like sesame oil that does not mix with water. He contemplates the realms of form and formlessness, observing their original non-existence and finding nothing to observe."

Manifesting in the formless realm, they are formless by nature, without posteriority or anteriority. They are like a flame that does not burn empty space; likewise, they neither increase nor diminish, neither come nor go, and have no place from which to depart or to which to arrive.
Walking alone through the three realms, they transcend the three states of existence, just as a flying bird traverses the void without any obstruction.
Delivering beings from the three realms according to their respective original aspirations, they cause them to quickly attain awakening and reach the Great Vehicle.

For example, it is like a king of physicians who possesses various medicines, each of which he administers according to the specific ailment so that diseases of wind, cold, or heat are immediately cured.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva uses the medicine of the Buddha-dharma to treat the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion until none remain; his mind becomes pure, formless, and nameless.

Just as a valiant and powerful general leads an army to suppress rebels and evildoers, so too does the Bodhisattva, through great compassion, transform and enlighten sentient beings. Those who wander in confusion, those of dull wit, those caught in the nets of the sixty-two views and various heterodox doubts, and those adhering to the sixty-two types of non-Dharmas—all are caused to resolve their minds, to personally observe the essentials of the six perfections and the practices of great kindness and great compassion, and are led to the Mahāyāna.
Just as a boatman steers a sturdy vessel to ferry all the common people back and forth, each according to their respective needs, so it is with the Bodhisattva.

By means of the samādhi of courageous subduing, they deliver beings from the afflictions of immeasurable birth and death; they manifest before śrāvakas to transform them according to their inclinations;

they manifest before pratyekabuddhas to provide instruction from the very beginning; they manifest the body of a Buddha to open the way of the three teachings; or they manifest the great Dharma of infinite wisdom and the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna, wherein there are neither the three evil realms nor the three vehicles.

For example, suppose a magician, in the midst of a great assembly, manifests his own death—being consumed by fire and devoured by beasts—and the multitude, all struck with terror, each seeks his mercy, offering him great gifts in the hope of restoring his body;
yet, knowing he has received many treasures, he rises from the ground and returns to his former state, for there was neither death nor resurrection.

In this way, the Bodhisattva transforms and guides sentient beings within the five paths of birth and death; he may manifest as a bodhisattva, or as a śrāvaka, or as a pratyekabuddha, or be born in the heavens. Suddenly appearing in nirvāṇa, the multitude weeps, saying he has been extinguished, yet he manifests entirely in other directions.

The pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas are also like this: they are said to have attained parinirvāṇa, as if nothing remains once a fire has been extinguished, having no fixed location and returning to the source of fire.

Although the Bodhisattva manifests Nirvana and merges with the Dharma-body, there is no coming or going; yet he returns to manifest himself in accordance with sentient beings to transform and deliver them—it is only the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who attains such realization!

To understand and know the Dharma-body is like the sun shining upon water, as well as upon kingdoms, counties, towns, hamlets, and villages; the solar palace neither descends nor moves, yet while remaining among humans, its light reaches everywhere without going or coming.

In this way, the bodhisattva manifests within the triple world yet neither comes nor goes, nor does he circulate therein; though he liberates all beings, there is nothing that is liberated. This is the samādhi of the valiant subduer.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of Surpassing the Radiance of the Sun, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Upper;
The Scripture on the Samādhi of Surpassing the Radiance of the Sun, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Western Jin lay devotee Nie Chengyuan.
Vimalanetra again addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is called the 'Sun-Transcending Radiance Samādhi'?
The Buddha replied, "Its radiance is immeasurable and beyond analogy, surpassing the light of the sun."

Why is this so? The brilliant light of the sun illuminates all present phenomena; humans, objects, crawling insects, the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, trees, and all the devas, nāgas, and spirits—all depend upon the sun to flourish and live.
The sun cannot illuminate the space between the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), nor can it illuminate the fundamental nature of the human mind to bring it to enlightenment.
It illuminates only that which has form, not that which is formless.
Why is the Samādhi of Surpassing Solar Radiance so superior?

Because its extraordinary illumination reaches the ten directions, boundless and limitless; throughout the three realms and the five paths of existence, there is nowhere it does not penetrate and clarify.

The Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva illuminates the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the ninety-six paths and the sixty-two views—dispelling the darkness of false doubts and fetters, causing their minds to suddenly awaken and all give rise to the aspiration for the Way. Those who practice the three vehicles each attain accomplishment; whether they are reborn in heaven or obtain a human body, there are none who do not universally receive this benefit.

It is like the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop Mount Sumeru, where the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and its purple-blue jeweled halls shine brilliantly above; below, in the four directions of the four heavenly kings' realms, dwell the various devas, humans, hungry ghosts, yakṣas, pretas, and various spirits.

The Samādhi of Transcendent Solar Radiance is likewise thus: the mind is firm and unmoving like Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains. It transforms the celestial kings of the five realms and Śakra, the Lord of Devas; it transcends the four heavenly kings by transforming birth, old age, sickness, and death. It heals all those who are unfilial and the defilements of lust, anger, and ignorance, causing them to resolve upon the Way. It causes those of the Lesser Vehicle to abandon their aims and turn toward the Great Vehicle. Whether they have already resolved upon the Way and received a prediction of enlightenment, or have not yet resolved upon it, they receive the prediction. They practice the six perfections to the ultimate degree, remaining entirely free of delusive thoughts, unaware even as they receive the prediction.
The Sun-Transcending Samādhi is most profound, most profound!
It is immeasurable and has no bottom or limit.

It is like space: even if someone were to attempt to measure space using measures such as *sheng*, *he*, *dou*, or *hu* to determine its volume, one might still be able to measure it exhaustively and know its quantity in *hu*; yet the wisdom of the Sun-Transcending Samādhi cannot be measured.

For example, suppose a person were to traverse the void for ten li, a hundred li, a thousand li, ten thousand li, a hundred million li, or even hundreds of billions of li—an immeasurable number of hundreds of nayutas of li. One might still be able to exhaustively reach the limits of that void; yet the radiance of the Sun-like Samādhi of Wisdom and Insight surpasses that by countless billions of times, doubling again and again beyond measure. When one attempts to create a metaphor for the radiance of the Way, it is neither distant nor near, neither broad nor narrow.
Vimalanetra asked the World-Honored One:
"The Great Sage has praised it as being extremely vast, immense, and far-reaching; why then do you say it is neither distant nor near, neither broad nor narrow?"
The Buddha said:

"Because there is narrowness, one speaks of width; because there is nearness, one speaks of distance. Where there is neither distance nor nearness, neither width nor narrowness, nothing can be used for comparison."

To provide a provisional analogy so that people may understand its boundlessness: it is like empty space, which transcends all limits without being outside them, and into which even formless atoms enter without being inside them;
there is no further calculation or comparison, for this analogy clarifies the ultimate meaning.

The wisdom of the Great Way is beyond comparison; it surpasses that of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, even reaching up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path. It is supreme, honored, peerless, and without equal. As a natural dharma, it has no creator and nothing that is not created; it neither comes nor goes, being empty, non-substantial, and spontaneous.

He thoroughly understands that all things are fundamentally non-existent; he thoroughly understands the beginning and end of all things. Having understood all these roots, he neither relies on anything nor does he not rely on anything; his spontaneous wisdom discerns and comprehends them all.

The three realms are spontaneous; the three realms being spontaneous, persons and things are spontaneous; persons and things being spontaneous, birth and death are spontaneous; birth and death being spontaneous, fundamental non-being is spontaneous; fundamental non-being being spontaneous, the Buddha-way is spontaneous. To understand and discern that all these are spontaneous, one is then able to attain the Samādhi of Transcending the Sun’s Radiance, universally saving those of the three periods of time and reaching infinite wisdom. This is called the Samādhi of Transcending the Sun’s Radiance.

At that time, there was a daughter of a householder named Prajñādattā, who came to the presence of the Buddha together with five hundred women. She prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and upon hearing the Buddha preach this *Sūryavairocana-samādhi*, she rejoiced immeasurably. She stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I, in my present female body, vow to give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. I wish to transform this female form, swiftly attain perfect awakening, and deliver all beings throughout the ten directions."
There was a bhikṣu named Shangdu who said to Huishī:
"One cannot attain the Buddha-way in a female body. Why is this so?..."
A woman has three things that separate her and five things that obstruct her.
What are the three?
In youth, she is controlled by her parents;
When a woman marries out, she loses her autonomy;
when she grows up, it is difficult for her to have children.
These are the three.
What are the five obstacles?
First, a woman cannot become Śakra. Why is this so?
One who is courageous and has few desires attains manhood; because of being mixed with evil and possessing many devious dispositions, one becomes a woman and cannot become Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
Second, one cannot become Brahmā.
Why is this so? Because by upholding pure conduct free from defilement and cultivating the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one who follows the four dhyānas ascends to the Brahma Heaven;
yet because of unrestrained lust and lack of moderation, one becomes a woman and cannot become a Brahma.
The third is: one must not become a Māra-deva.

Why is this? Only by fully practicing the ten wholesome deeds, revering the Triple Gem, serving one's two parents with filial piety, and being humble and compliant toward elders does one attain the status of a Māra-deva.
Because they were arrogant, disrespectful, and disparaged the True Teaching, they became women and could not become Māra-devas;
fourthly, they could not become Universal Monarchs (cakravartin).

Why is this so? By practicing the Bodhisattva path with compassion for all sentient beings, and by reverently supporting the Three Jewels, former sages, and teachers, one may become a Wheel-Turning King who rules over the four continents, teaching the people to universally practice the ten wholesome deeds and honoring the Way and its Virtue as a Dharma King’s instruction.
However, because she concealed eighty-four modes of conduct and lacked pure practice, she became a woman; thus, she could not become a holy sovereign emperor.
The fifth point is that women cannot become Buddhas. Why is this?

One becomes a Buddha only after practicing the bodhicitta with compassion for all beings, donning the armor of the Mahāyāna through great kindness and great compassion, eliminating the five aggregates (*skandha*) and transforming the six decays (*āyatana*), extensively cultivating the six perfections (*pāramitā*), and realizing profound wisdom. One must practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; transcend the three gates of liberation; understand the non-existence of self, person, life-span, or soul; and comprehend the fundamental non-arising of dharmas through the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). One must discern that all things are like illusions, transformations, dreams, shadows, clusters of plantain trees, froth on water, mirages, lightning flashes, and the moon reflected in water—essentially non-existent in these five locations and devoid of the perception of the three realms of rebirth. Only then can one attain Buddhahood.

Yet, because they are attached to form and desire, their passions are turbid and their demeanors are hidden; since their body, speech, and mind are discordant, they become women and cannot become Buddhas.
Those who possess these five conditions all have their origins and conclusions.
Then, the girl Prajñādattā replied to Upatiṣya:
"Each plants various roots to obtain their respective fruits; do these roots possess male or female characteristics, or do they have karmic retribution?"
"Are there originally five places for Śakra, Brahmā, the Māra King, the Wheel-Turning Sage Emperor,
the Great Way, and the Small Way? Shangdu replied,
"There are none."
Huishī asked: "If it were originally non-existent, by what cause would it come to be?
He replied:
"It is accomplished through causal practice.

Huidi replied, "It is like a painter who prepares his walls, boards, and canvases, and gathers his pigments; by following a model, he applies the colors and, according to his intention, the image is completed."
The five paths of existence are likewise!
Originally they have no fixed location; they are formed according to one's actions.

It is like a master illusionist who conjures the sun and moon, Śakra, Brahmā, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, humans, birds, and beasts; these appear at will, yet in an instant of bewilderment, their location is unknown.
Birth and death are thus!
Fundamentally they do not exist; they arise from the activities of the mind, and each person attains them for themselves.
Upon reaching that fundamental non-existence—where there is no illusion and no transformation, no joining and no dispersing, and no location—one then attains Buddhahood!

Why is this so? By observing the five precepts one becomes human; by practicing the ten wholesome actions one is born in heaven; through stinginess one falls among the hungry ghosts; through violence one is reborn as an animal; and through evil deeds one falls into hell.
By practicing the four immeasurable minds but failing to understand the practice of emptiness, one is born in the Brahma Heaven.
Relying on emptiness to seek deliverance, with a distracted mind attached to emptiness, one is born in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

Although one possesses the thought of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), this thought does not transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*). Fearing suffering and loathing the body, detesting the hardships of birth and death, and setting one's will upon *nirvāṇa*, one consequently falls to the stage of an Arhat.

Having resolved to become a Bodhisattva to deliver all beings, yet failing to understand that [all things] are fundamentally non-existent and becoming attached to the physical marks of a Buddha’s body, one desires to quickly attain Buddhahood; however, lacking a good teacher and failing to comprehend skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one halts midway and attains the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
If that which one practices involves both conjunction and separation, then one cannot achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Since all things are without marks (*animitta*), how can there be male or female?
Shangdu asked again:
"By what kind of practice does one achieve perfect enlightenment?
Huishishi replied:
There is no practice of the arising of form, no practice of contemplating it as non-empty, no practice of the cessation of form, and no practice of abandoning or creating it.

There is no practice of the arising of consciousness, no practice of contemplating it as non-empty, and no practice of the cessation of consciousness. There is no practice of the arising of form, no practice of the arising of consciousness, nor is there any practice of returning, coming, or going; there is forever no location, and no practice of abiding anywhere.

Not leaning upon the three realms, neither abandoning nor grasping the five aggregates; not abandoning worldly conduct and not conceptualizing the conduct of the Path—this is the practice of the Path that leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

Not relying on the four immeasurables, not conceptualizing the practices of the six perfections, and not relying on any practice within the three gates of liberation, one realizes the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is the bodhisattva’s practice that accords with the Dharma and does not contradict the impartial conduct of perfect enlightenment.
"O Superior One!
For one who practices this Dharma, could there be any direction, location, or the three realms of male and female?
He replied:
"There is none. Since there is not even a creator, what could possibly be established?
"For this reason, what difficulty is there in my taking up the Buddha?
To take up that which is not taken up, to accomplish that which is not accomplished, to awaken to that which is not awakened—to have neither grasping nor abandoning—is what is called 'Buddha'."
"Furthermore, there is no name or title; it is merely a provisional designation!
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"O Hui-shi!
It is exactly as you have said.

All things are accomplished through non-attainment; they are neither conjoined nor dispersed, neither arising nor decaying. Being without seeing or hearing, without thought or cognition, and without speech or explanation, one thereby attains perfect enlightenment."

Thereupon, Prajñādattā transformed her female form into that of a man; she leaped into the air and descended from above, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the five hundred women leaped for joy and spoke in verse:
"We have always observed ourselves, Thinking that men possess a constant seed;
Strength and weakness each have their own category, And women are certainly unable to change it."
Today, having received the Buddha’s grace, I have come to know that nothing is solid;
the five realms of existence are like illusions and transformations, each formed according to one's own karma.
The three worlds arise from the delusions of the mind, for one fails to realize the truth of original non-existence.
Self-conceitedly calculating that there is a self, one is bound and falls into the mire.
Just as a fisherman catches fish with a hook,
[the mind] seizes what is not its own, yet claims, "I shall obtain this."
The three realms are like a temporary lodging; the four great elements are not mine.
Understanding all phenomena to be like dreams, there is then nothing to grasp or reject.
May the Buddha alone look upon me with compassion; may his kindness and mercy cover me as a canopy.
May she transform her female body, Encounter the Samādhi of Surpassing Solar Radiance,
Attain Buddhahood and establish a land, To teach and transform all devas and humans;
May all sentient beings be delivered and liberated, Swiftly attaining the unsurpassed truth.
The Buddha told the five hundred women:
"May you swiftly attain your aspirations as you have wished.
The women were filled with joy, and they immediately became men.
Thereupon, the Buddha bestowed upon Prajñādatta and her five hundred women the prediction:

"Ten kalpas hence, you shall all become Buddhas, named Prajñādarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha Bhagavān."
The world was called Dispelling Darkness, and the eon was called Radiance.

The Buddha remained for hundreds of billions of years preaching the Dharma; Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the patience of non-arising, and those in their final birth before Buddhahood were likewise innumerable, while Arhats were beyond all calculation.
At that time, the clothing and food of the people shall be like those in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When the assembled multitude heard the Buddha bestow this prediction, one hundred thousand people or more conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; countless bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; eighty thousand bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; and for one hundred thousand devas and humans, the dust was removed and defilements cleansed, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose.

The earth shook violently, flowers scattered from the air falling like rain, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Hundreds of millions of devas in the sky all uttered praises, saying:
"How profound is this Dharma!"
It is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear.
How fortunate we are!
Having possessed residual merit from past lives, we now encounter and hear it; how joyful this is!
The Buddha again addressed Hui-shi:

"When people in this world are bound by the cycle of birth and death, it is solely because they do not understand the profound Dharma and instead calculate in terms of 'self,' 'person,' and 'individual. This is like the gibbon who was enticed and deceived by wine; knowing he could not escape, he was captured by men."

The people of the world are like this: entangled in the afflictions of the five aggregates and the six sense-decays, they constantly calculate in terms of "self" and "mine. They do not realize that all things are suffering, empty, selfless, and not a body; thus, when they transgress, they incur calamity yet fail to restrain themselves. Bound by the three poisons and the five hindrances, they cannot attain liberation or return to the path of ultimate truth.

Just as fire produced from wood does not realize it is burning itself, so too is it with those who do not understand the practice of emptiness but instead calculate in terms of "I," "self," and "person"; they thus deceive themselves, falling into darkness and entering the three evil realms.
It is like a violent bandit who plunders and harms others, yet considers himself strong and capable.

So too, worldly people become attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they sink into defilement, sin, obscurations, and hindrances. Failing to understand the sublime, profound, and wondrous meaning of the Great Dharma, and being possessed by ignorance and craving, they are born as human beings.
The twelve fetters and sixty-two views, the net of doubt with its fine meshes, and the ninety-six heterodox paths that delude all—

having refined one's essence through all dharmas and discerned their emptiness and non-existence, one sees them as like illusions, transformations, dreams, plantain trees, mirages, the moon in water, or the echo of a shout, and thus does not conceive of a self.

One knows that form is naturally so, and sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are naturally so; that mental formations and consciousness are naturally so, and the four great elements are naturally so; that the four great elements are naturally so, and the three realms are naturally so; that the three realms are naturally so, and nirvāṇa is naturally so. When one realizes that nirvāṇa is naturally so, one is then able to attain the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Abiding neither in birth-and-death nor dwelling in extinction, one thus accords with the profound and wondrous wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

It is like a person whose body has contracted a grave illness who, wishing to treat it himself, should take a medicine that suits his condition but instead drinks a poisonous drug; this attacks the physical frame, harming the abdomen and injuring the internal organs. If he does not immediately take a powder to eliminate the poison, it will soon kill him, and by then there will be no time for regret.
It is the same for those who study the Way!

Having originally resolved upon the aspiration for enlightenment to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, they uphold the four immeasurable minds—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and observe the six perfections; yet, because they harbor conceptualizations and have expectations, they fall into the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Even if they should happen to achieve [realization], they do not delight in emerging from it; though they reach the Mahāyāna, they hesitate and lack clarity, and by dwelling in this intermediate state, they fall into the Lesser Vehicle.
For example, the food of a commoner would be like a poisonous drug to a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
For example, ambrosia is the supreme flavor and a complete medicine that cures many of the ailments of the multitude.
So it is with the Bodhisattva!

By means of the Mahāyāna Dharma, they extensively provide healing for all people from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, lust, anger, and ignorance, as well as from the calamities of manifold conceptualizations.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, one thousand devas conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and five hundred sons of gods attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Huiying (Wisdom-Essence).
He asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being widely learned and possessed of great knowledge? Mañjuśrī replied:
“From incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have accumulated merit without weariness;
hearing of the four immeasurable minds, they are never satiated; practicing the four methods of benevolence, they are never satiated; performing the six perfections, they are never satiated;
and regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they are never satiated. Great compassion and...”
They never tire of compassion; they never tire of advancing toward the five supernormal powers; they never tire of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
they never tire of the Mahāyāna teachings; they never tire of manifesting as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to universally transform all;
nor do they tire of manifesting parinirvāṇa, dwelling within nirvāṇa, and yet returning to the realm of saṃsāra.
Without weariness or satiety, neither departing nor arriving, there is nowhere it does not reach;

just as space reaches everywhere, it neither emerges nor enters, yet there is nowhere it does not penetrate and nowhere it does not pervade. This is what is called being widely learned and possessing great knowledge.
One does not reckon by means of the past, nor does one encounter limitations through the future, nor does one find a fixed location in the present.

Being free from the constraints of the three periods of past, future, and present, one regards the three miserable realms as equal, harbors no conception of the three worlds, and entertains no thought of nirvana. Having neither the path nor the mundane, one neither clings to nor rejects them; this is what is called being widely learned and possessing great knowledge.

In that which is heard, there is nothing heard; in that which is seen, there is nothing seen; in that which is spoken, there is nothing spoken; in that which is delivered, there is nothing delivered. This is what is called being widely learned and possessing great wisdom.
Huiying asked again:
"What is meant by 'the practitioner' (xingzhe)?
What is meant by 'accomplishment' (chengjiu)?"
He replied:

"One who gives rise to the bodhicitta and practices the four immeasurable minds, possessing the wisdom of great kindness and great compassion, gathering in others through giving, and saving sentient beings through precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—progressing gradually in these practices—is called a practitioner.

One whose practice transcends the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, seeing neither self nor others, neither the three periods of time, nor nirvana and samsara, is called one who has attained accomplishment."
The Bodhisattva Dàying again asked the Buddha:
“From where does a human being come?
To where does one go?”
From where do old age, sickness, and death come?
To where do they go?
From what do form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise?
Where do they go?
From where do earth, water, fire, wind, space, the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind come?
Where do they go?
The Buddha said:

"They all come from nowhere and go nowhere; when conditions combine they arise, and when conditions separate they cease. They are like illusions, like transformations, like paintings, like drums, like rain, and like lightning—all arise from causes and conditions."
"Where there is a condition, there is birth; where there is no condition, there is no opposition. Birth and death are thus, being equal and without difference.
Da Ying asked again:
"What is meant by 'coming from nowhere and going nowhere, yet being formed through the synthesis of causes and conditions'?"

The Buddha said: "One who performs the deeds of a human becomes a human; one who performs the deeds of a deva becomes a deva; one who performs the deeds of hell enters hell; one who performs the deeds of an animal receives birth as an animal; and one who performs the deeds of a hungry ghost becomes a hungry ghost."
Without the five elements, there are no five destinies; without the five destinies, there is no coming or going—this is called the human root.

There are no three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—because there is no mind, intellect, or consciousness; thus there are no three realms, which is called the human root.
There has never been a person or thing that possesses form but lacks visibility.
What is meant by "possessing form but lacking visibility"?

It refers to the form of earth, the form of water, the form of fire, and the form of wind. That which is stable is called earth; that which is clear is called water; that which is luminous is called fire; and that which is cohesive is called wind.

Before heaven and earth existed, and before the three realms had yet come into being, these four form-essences were eternally spontaneous; they arose naturally without a creator, and only the Way can name them, as can those who have reached the stage of the "Place of Rebirth" (Upapadya).
This is the color of formlessness, which is also called the color of the mind.

The Avaivartika sees the mind and the color of the mind; the Avinipāta sees the four colors of the mind; and the Tathāgata sees the fundamental source of the four colors of the mind that have not yet arisen.
That which does not burn within the three realms is the mind-and-form (nāmarūpa) of the mind; it is called the "root of the mind," and therefore it is said that it is not "not burning.
Because it pertains to the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, it is said to be "burning."
When the mind is absent and the will regarding form is naturally extinguished within the three realms, and this natural state is like empty space, it is called the Way (*dharma*).
Thus, all phenomena are neither joined nor dispersed. Why is this so?
If they are conjoined, it is the fundamental nature of man; if they are dispersed, it is birth and death.
One who perceives the suffering of birth and death and the bliss of Nirvāṇa is called a Śrāvaka.
Abiding in the middle, benefiting all without exception, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
Being neither joined nor dispersed, neither dwelling in nirvana nor loathing birth-and-death, this is what is termed the Dharma-body.
"The Dharma-body is formless and universally enters all things; yet it neither enters anything nor does it not enter anything.

When this sutra was spoken, five thousand devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and incalculable numbers of people all resolved to attain supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Thereupon Ānanda asked the World-Honored One:
"For one who wishes to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment as a bodhisattva, what should be taken as the foundation?
The Buddha said:
“Diligently and without slackening, one discriminates the wisdom of emptiness, desiring to deliver all beings; not perceiving a self or a life-span—this is the foundation.
He asked again:
“Is there any slowness or swiftness [in this]?”
The Buddha said,
"Both existent and non-existent.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'existence' (bhava)?
What is meant by 'non-existence' (abhava)?
The Buddha said:

"Existence arises from diligence and non-laxity; by accumulating merit through generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and skillful means, as well as the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, the four debts of gratitude, and the practice of emptiness, one attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path. This is not attained through laxity; this is what is meant by 'existence'."
As for "non-existence" (*wu*): the Way has no location, no form, and no name; it is like empty space, which cannot be attained through conditioned activity.

It is without anything created, without mind, thought, or consciousness; it is neither internal nor external, nor is there a middle between them. To neither grasp nor reject is to accord with entry into the Way—this is what is meant by "non-existence."
Why is this so? In the distant past, through kalpas too numerous to calculate, there was a wheel-turning king named Īśvara.

He had a thousand sons, brave and extraordinary; he ruled over the four continents as the lord of the seven treasures of the realm, governing by the True Dharma without the application of punishments.
At that time there was a Buddha, titled Ratnakusuma Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma; it was excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its conclusion.
He analyzed its meaning with subtle and complete perfection, purely cultivating the holy life and extensively expounding the Dharma.
At that time, there were countless billions of bodhisattvas in the assembly, and śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas beyond measure.

Then, the Wheel-Turning King, having served and made offerings to the Buddha for many years, accompanied by his thousand sons, precious ministers, and a great multitude, proceeded together to the Buddha’s dwelling. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha then expounded for him extensively upon the conduct of a bodhisattva—how it brings great peace and security and provides vast protection, making the bodhisattva the most honored among all beings.

The king, his sons, the precious ministers, and their retinue all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; they practiced with diligence day and night, never daring to grow weary or rest, providing for the Tathāgata all that he required for his comfort.

Thereupon, the thousand sons all tested their own merits before the Buddha, each drawing a lot to determine who would become a Buddha first. He who drew the superior lot would be followed by the others in descending order until those of inferior merit; the most indolent and of the thinnest virtue would be the very last to attain Buddhahood.
Then, as instructed, each of them drew a lot.
One prince drew the last lot; having reached the very bottom of the ranking, he was destined to become a Buddha last of all.
At that moment, he was overcome with grief and could not restrain himself; he threw himself down like a great mountain collapsing, crying out, "How can my body be the last to attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha told him: "Do not be distressed;
the Way has no limits, nor does it have distance or nearness. Once you are able to discern and understand the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence, it will be right before you!"

At that time, upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the Prince immediately leaped for joy and gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). He attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*), practiced great compassion, and understood that all phenomena are like illusions, echoes, and shadows; like a mirage, a dream, a plantain tree, or the moon reflected in water. Among a thousand people, he was the fourth to attain Buddhahood, being named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"The remaining sons shall attain Buddhahood in succession;
the last one to become a Buddha shall be named Luyou.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who the Wheel-Turning Sage King was at that time, it was the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
As for Prince Prajñākūṭa, he understood emptiness and non-substantiality, and through diligent and untiring effort, he was the first to attain Buddhahood; that person was none other than myself."
The remaining sons are those who will appear as the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.

You should understand this principle: the Way has no distance; it is only by realizing emptiness, discerning the sublime, and knowing the naturally spontaneous Dharma that one attains Buddhahood swiftly.

At that time, there was no one among the assembly who was not filled with joy; they all resolved their minds on the Way and practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva. Five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and ten thousand people attained the patience of compliance with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti).

Then, on that day, the Sun Deity (Āditya-rāja), together with incalculable hundreds of thousands of devas, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what practice does the Sun Deity perform the act of illuminating the four continents?"
"For what reason does the moon serve as the moon, illuminating the night and dispelling the darkness?
The Buddha told the Sun King:
"There are four dharmas by which one becomes the Sun King."
What are the four? Constantly delighting in giving;

cultivating the body and being careful in conduct while reverently upholding the precepts without transgression; furthermore, vowing to light lamps at Buddhist temples and shrines, or planting the merit of radiance for one's parents, śramaṇas, and practitioners of the Way;
these are the four.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Always delight in practicing generosity, Uphold the precepts and do not transgress prohibitions;
Light lamps in Buddhist temples, Or before one's parents."
Delighting in the Buddha’s true scriptures, Not slandering the sutras and the Dharma;
Revering śramaṇas and seekers of the Way— By these causes, one becomes a sun.
From his body issue a thousand rays of light, Universally illuminating the four continents.
"In all places of profound darkness, there is none that does not receive its brilliant radiance.
The Buddha told the Sun King:
"Furthermore, there are ten matters by which one becomes a Sun Heavenly King."
What are the ten?

The body does not commit killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; the mouth does not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, or frivolous chatter; and the mind is free from malice, envy, and delusion.
These are the ten.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Reverently compose yourself and guard your own conduct, Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
Avoiding double-tongued speech, harsh words, Falsehoods, and frivolous chatter."
"The mind harbors no envy, And is free from the poisons of anger and hatred;
Having abandoned the sixty-two views, The light of the sun illuminates the four quarters.
The Buddha said to the Sun King:
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one may become a Moon King.
What are these four? They are:
bestowing alms upon the poor and destitute; upholding the five precepts; revering the Three Jewels; and secretly providing lamps for the shrines of one's sovereign, father, teacher, and monastery."
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Bestowing gifts upon those who are poor and destitute, and constantly upholding the five precepts;"
Lighting lamps in Buddhist temples, one reverently serves the Triple Gem;
with a mind mindful of all that is good, one eliminates the manifold evils of the world;
by guarding one’s own body, speech, and mind, one attains the moonlight that illuminates the darkness.
At that time, King Divākara addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the Great Sage would deign to visit my palace for a light meal, so that all the guiding deities and celestial beings of the void may receive great grace; hearing this profound and wondrous Dharma, may they all resolve to attain the Way, and those delivered thereby may be immeasurable."
At that time, the Buddha accepted his invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the Buddha had consented to attend the feast, King Divākara circumambulated the Buddha three times and suddenly returned to his palace. There he prepared a hundred kinds of food of various sweet flavors, and arranged beds, couches, and seating with exquisite and pure adornment; for the sake of the Buddha, he spread out a seat four thousand *li* in height.
On that day, the King stood in his palace, bowing from afar with deep reverence and holding his breath in awe, praising the Buddha in verse:
"Bestowing gifts upon all, Without begrudging anything he possessed;
Furthermore, not hoping for any recompense, He has attained Buddhahood to deliver the ten directions."
Your wisdom is like space, and those you transform are without hindrance;
all receive your grace, and now that the time has come, we pray you will deign to descend.
You bestow compassion upon all sentient beings and have never caused them harm.
To those who have not yet crossed over sorrow, you bestow instruction with the treasure of the Dharma;
with your majestic spiritual power, you illuminate the masses and rescue those who are destitute;
you grant them the seven great riches—now that the time has come, we pray only that you deign to descend.
Beholding sentient beings in delusion, suffering the hardships of the five realms of existence,
he constantly bestows great compassion upon them, consoling and encouraging those who are terrified.
He transforms them through the teachings of the Dharma, guiding those who have not yet reached understanding.
The seeds have reached emptiness and lack wisdom; the time has come, so please deign to bend your majesty.
His radiance surpasses the sun and moon; his majestic virtue exceeds Mount Sumeru;
his wisdom transcends space—these two cannot be compared by any analogy.
The sun and moon illuminate all darkness, yet they can only bring the myriad things to fruition;
the Buddha illuminates those on the five paths, causing them all to obtain the five eyes.
One might as well measure the void, or know how many drops there are in the ocean’s waters; [but the Buddha’s merit is beyond such reckoning].
The lands of the ten directions, even Mount Sumeru, may have their weight measured;
yet the sagely wisdom of the Tathāgata is vast and towering in its merit.
Boundlessly surpassing all else, the time has come—please deign to descend.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"The time has come; all preparations are complete. Proceed to the invitation of the Sun-King.
Thereupon, they all received his instruction.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, leaped into the void and proceeded to the palace of King Divākara, where they sat upon lion thrones.

Once the assembly had taken their seats, the queen, the crown prince, and the various celestial retinues prostrated themselves upon the ground. With sincere hearts, they made offerings to the World-Honored One; with their own hands, they served a hundred kinds of delicacies. When the meal was finished and they had washed their hands, they took lower seats and sat before the Buddha, listening to the Dharma with reverent solemnity.
The Buddha told King Sūrya:

"All physical forms experienced within the three realms arise from the mind and its intentions. Though the mind and intentions have no form, they create and follow through with actions that establish the person. Whether noble and wealthy or poor and lowly, all return to impermanence; like a bubble that arises and then instantly collapses, so it is with everything in the world!"
One should believe that the Way and its Virtue (moral truth) are the true and genuine refuge; nothing else can be relied upon. Abandoning all other practices, one should practice the Dharma-conduct.
What is meant by Dharma-conduct?

It is the practice of non-arising, which eliminates all that arises; it is the practice of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), which is preeminent in what it preserves, and through which one enters the Path.
In the practice of conduct, there is nothing forgotten or lost; in the practice of giving, there is no stinginess or expectation;

in the practice of precept-keeping, all vows are universally fulfilled; in the practice of patience, one does not disturb the multitude; in the practice of diligence, there is never any wavering or turning back;
in the practice of single-mindedness, the mental activity is always penetrating; and in the practice of wisdom, one beholds with the noble eye.
The practice of loving-kindness endures all suffering; the practice of compassion regards all sentient beings with an equal mind;
the practice of sympathetic joy transforms others through the Dharma; the practice of equanimity comforts all; the practice of supernormal powers attains the sixfold penetration;
the practice of contemplating emptiness is free from anger and malice; and the practice of eradication brings about deliverance.
The practice of the four debts of gratitude for all sentient beings gathers together to save them; the practice of extensive learning leads to the attainment of the Way through reception;
the practice of non-arising contemplates the natural state; the practice of the factors of enlightenment does not grasp at conditioned existence;
the practice of primordial non-being has no retribution of sin or merit; and the practice of dependent origination thoroughly understands that ignorance is ungraspable and cannot be known.
Exhausting all wearisome practices, one understands that persons and things are spontaneous; through the practice of all dharmas, one realizes emptiness and attains the wisdom of equal enlightenment.
In the practice of subduing Māra, one cannot be shaken; though dwelling within the field of the three realms, one does not fall.
With the lion-like practice of supreme victory and fearlessness, one possesses the power of fearlessness such that there is no dread in whatever direction one turns.

The practice of the threefold penetration is free from all obstructions; with a single-minded field of awakening, great wisdom is universally complete, and the teaching of all practices reaches everywhere.
He transforms those who hold the sixty-two views to deliver them from the net of suffering, and instructs those on the ninety-six paths to enter the One Way.

"Thus it is, O King of the Sun! When a bodhisattva accords with these practices, they are practicing in accordance with the Way. Having practiced in accordance with the Way, they accord with great kindness (*maitrī*); having accorded with great kindness, they accord with great compassion (*karuṇā*); having accorded with great compassion, they accord with the great armor; having accorded with the great armor, they utter the lion’s roar; having uttered the lion’s roar, they accord with the transformation of illusions; having accorded with the transformation of illusions, they enter the five realms of existence; having accorded with the five realms of existence, they enter them according to the occasion; having entered according to the occasion, there is nothing that does not transform; and being within that which transforms, there is neither going nor coming."
"To deliver that which is not delivered, to purify that which is not purified, to illuminate that which is not illuminated, and to awaken to that which is not awakened—this is true awakening.
The Buddha told King Sun:

"If you wish to penetrate the matters of the past, future, and present, and to realize the equality of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the ten directions, you should always with faith and joy discern this meaning."

If you wish to know from whence arise the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda), the afflictions of the three realms of existence, and the shrouds of the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa), you should understand this meaning and practice it with faith.

If you wish to comprehend the essentials of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana), to open the teaching of the threefold penetration, to transcend the three liberations (trivimokṣa), and to attain the wisdom of the threefold penetration, you must understand this meaning.

Just as the various provinces, counties, towns, hamlets, villages, and settlements, as well as the hundred grains, grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, and fruit-bearing plants, all grow depending upon the earth;

so too, when a Bodhisattva enters this wisdom, there is nothing they do not transform, establishing all beings until they reach the path of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, such that both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas rely upon it as their foundation.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the King of the Sun Devas, his queen, his crown prince, their retinues, and all the devas spontaneously attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); one billion devas and humans resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and stood in mid-air, surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of followers. He spoke in verse:
“Gods and humans do not understand, That which has long been difficult to measure;
They are deluded within the five realms of existence, Like fish caught on a hook and bait.”
The three realms are like an illusion, Vague and indistinct, with no place to be found;
Beings do not realize this themselves, Driven instead by the power of consciousness.
Falling into the four inversions, They are truly to be pitied and commiserated.
One reckons for oneself that the body is permanent, and does not believe in the truth of the Way.
All things arise from emptiness, yet one instead hates and refuses to hear the wisdom of emptiness;
it is like a person born of their parents who, in turn, is unfilial toward them.
When a dog is transformed into a tiger, it is not aware of its former human state;
soon it returns to harm its own household, making no distinction between kin and stranger.
Human beings originally arise from emptiness; their hatred for what does not exist is likewise so!
Deluded regarding the aggregates and sense bases, one is like a drunkard running about naked;
when the phantom changes into a human, one recognizes family and kin;
once one discerns that these were originally non-existent, one understands that all things are empty.
The empty does not conceive of emptiness, nor does emptiness perceive emptiness;
having reached the state where nothing arises, one is then able to understand spontaneity.
Those who seek the bodhisattva practice to deliver and liberate the multitudes of sentient beings—
Having fully realized that all phenomena are naturally like illusions and transformations,
once one has distinguished this wisdom,
one moves through the world without difficulty.
"Thus they enter deeply into the subtle and profound, using skillful means and wisdom to deliver and transform beings.

When the Buddha spoke these words, countless billions of devas and various deities in the void all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Buddha then returned to the Amra Grove of the Mallas at Vaiśālī.

At that time, there was a great elder in the city named Haidu (解法度), who had made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of previous Buddhas; he had planted immeasurable roots of merit and had prostrated before and paid boundless homage to all Buddhas. Having received and accepted their Dharma teachings, his resolve for the unsurpassed, right, and true path was non-retrogressive. Possessing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and having emerged through wisdom, his practice of the infinite perfections (*pāramitā*) and his deliverance through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) were beyond calculation.

Accompanied by his retinue, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, sat to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha: "What merit is obtained by making offerings to the World-Honored One?"
The Buddha told the householder:
“By offering flowers and scattering them over the Buddha, you will be handsome and upright in every birth, and clothing and food will appear spontaneously before you.
By burning incense that wafts its fragrance, your body will be pure and fragrant, and your fame and virtue will be heard afar.”
Those who light lamps will possess the clear wisdom of the divine eye and shall not dwell in darkness;
those who offer banners and streamers will find wealth, joy, and infinite treasures wherever they go;
those who offer fine silk canopies will attain houses and dwellings that provide full shelter and protection from the elements.
By offering music and performing dances for Buddhist stūpas and monasteries, and by delighting all beings with music, one attains the divine ear of far-reaching hearing;
by giving shoes and vehicles, one attains lightness of body and the ability to fly;
and by directing the single mind toward the Buddha, one gains knowledge of past lives.
Through loving-kindness, one observes sentient beings and knows all their minds;
by giving the gift of Dharma, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows;
by giving the gift of food, one constantly encounters assemblies of the Dharma.
By giving clothing as an offering, one obtains the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
after my parinirvāṇa, whoever makes offerings to images or relics shall likewise possess such merit!
"By gradually conforming to the Dharma, one thereby attains the Way of Unconditioned Nirvana.
The Elder Jiefah (Kṣemadatta) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any offering that surpasses these flowers, incense, banners, canopies, music, shoes, carriages, food, and clothing?"
The Buddha said, "There are.
He asked again:
"What is this? The Buddha said:
